title.en: Space Marine 2 gets a massive anniversary update

summary.en: Celebrate the start of Year 3 with a new weapon and play as Chaos Space Marines in Siege Mode.

content.en:
A new update is out today for Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine 2, with a new weapon, new chances to play as dastardly heretics, and new challenges for the most daring players.
Let’s start with the new Champion pack. The Space Wolves send one of their best with an incredible new armour set based on the Wolf Guard Battle Leader, complete with a round Fenrisian storm shield so you can use it with the Bulwark class.
This modified MkX Tacticus suit is covered in furs and fangs befitting one of the Chapter’s most storied veterans.
But wait, what’s that he’s holding up there? From today, players can bash xenos skulls in and sunder Rubric power armour with a mighty one-handed thunder hammer! This brutal weapon is faster than the two-handed variant and can charge up to deal rippling area-of-effect blows, making it a great option for all kinds of foes.
Players using the Tactical, Assault, Bulwark, and Techmarines classes can all take the one-handed thunder hammer into battle, and there’s even a powerful Heroic version – the Power Maul.
These come alongside top-end additions for the power axe, auto bolt rifle, and five new cosmetic items bought with Accolades, including a fancy shoulderpad for the Black Templars and an Iron Halo.
The Tactical class is getting a top-to-bottom rework in this patch, renovating large swathes of its skill tree to offer more varied and interesting build options. It will also be getting access to the one-handed thunder hammer, the power axe, and the power sword, though with any of these powerful melee options equipped, you’ll lose access to your primary weapon.
So what if you want to take a bolt rifle and a power axe? There’s actually a Signature Perk for that – replacing the old Signal Jammer, you’ll now be able to choose an option that lets you take the regular, humble bolt rifle in your secondary weapon slot, with progression shared with its normal primary slot version. Tactical specialists really are the most versatile Space Marines in the squad.
If you’re looking for more of a challenge to test out the new skills, or simply enjoy running through Operations as close to the wire as possible, try out the new Crucible mode to earn Crucible XP. By talking to the Company Chaplain on board the battle barge you can activate Penances – personal debuffs that make your run harder – and completing missions with them active will put you on track to earning a set of Lamenters armour pieces.
Alongside the Space Wolves Champion Pack, the mysterious Exorcists Chapter also gets a Cosmetic Pack added to the Season Pass. This set of stylised armour pieces includes one Helmet, two Left and Right Pauldrons, two Left and Right Gauntlets, and one Breastplate from everyone’s favourite daemon-hunting Successor Chapter, covered in purity seals and arcane script. The Space Wolves Champion pack and Exorcists Chapter Pack are available to buy individually and also as part of Season Pass 3, whilst everything else included in the update is free.
Fancy getting a bit traitorous? A new spin on the wave-based Siege mode lets you step into the boots of a Chaos Space Marine to slaughter Tyranids, Imperial Guardsmen, and even loyalist Space Marines as you fight for dominion over Avarax. The new mode will initially include two sectors, with a third planned for a later release.
On top of all of this, we’ve still got room for a few more free additions. Heroic weapon variants of the power axe, one-handed thunder hammer, and auto bolt rifle will be added to the armoury, along with five new armour pieces and an expansion of the wargear sharing system. A third slot will open up to be used with capes, tabards, and iron halos, while some new items for Vanguard, Heavy, and Assault classes can be unlocked with new Ordeals.
This is only the first big update coming over the next 12 months, and the Year 3 battle plan is stacked with enough new content to fill a battle barge, from new weapons and new operations to an entirely new class – the Apothecary! Check out our first look at the schedule.
And that just about covers it! Head into Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine 2 now to try out the new update, and get yourself prepared for Year 3.

title.en: This toolless modular lever-action wallet is the coolest I’ve stuck to my phone

summary.en: The OhSnap Wallet 2 is a lever-action aluminum wallet with stackable modular parts, so a three card pocket wallet can transform into a seven card magnet one!

content.en:
This toolless modular lever-action wallet is the coolest I’ve stuck to my phone.
This toolless modular lever-action wallet is the coolest I’ve stuck to my phone
Pull the lever to fan your cards with the OhSnap Wallet 2.
Remember when I tested the ultra-thin and convenient OhSnap Snap Grip Stand and liked it so much I bought my own? Now, OhSnap has a magnetic lever-action card wallet that can stack with that stand. It’s the coolest wallet I’ve ever stuck to my phone.
Pull the integrated springy lever, and your cards fan out. Want a thicker or thinner wallet? Press in the right place and it comes apart without tools, letting you swap in a 3, 5, or 7-card “core” that grips your cards so they don’t fall out.
Want an ID card, work badge, elastic band for more cards, or a money clip on the end? You can change out the front or back magnetic plates for any of those. Or, change out both for ultra-thin aluminum covers if you don’t need the wallet to magnetically stick to your phone.
You can see it in action in my Today I’m Toying With video embedded in this post (also on YouTube and on Instagram if you prefer).
My favorite part is that the whole kit snaps together using a compliant mechanism — the plastic arms of the card-carrying core act like springs, pushing a little locking mechanism into the notches of each modular cover you add as you slide the parts together. Once your cards are inside, they keep the arms apart so it can’t open accidentally (unless you drop the entire wallet). It’s all very clever.
Even when I did drop the wallet (thanks for the suggestion, hugo!), it didn’t explode, typically. Usually, it just came apart slightly, though I did drop it hard on concrete one time and was able to make a small explosion: one half popped off, and two cards came out, but everything landed in a two-foot radius. The wallet has a big dent now.
There are definitely some downsides. While OhSnap advertises the Wallet 2 as “impossibly thin,” it’s only truly surprisingly sleek in its thinnest 3-card variant, without the thicker and heavier MagSafe and MagStack (which lets you snap other magnets to it) plates attached.
But the reason I’m not buying one is the price and weight. The 7-card version makes my phone feel too heavy, adding 127 grams, and while I happily made the 3-card my wallet for a few weeks, it’d cost me $61 on Kickstarter or $76 retail to get that with a double-magnet kit. OhSnap’s also charging more than I’d like ($35 for an ID cover or a money clip!) for extras.
OhSnap didn’t get me this time. But I could see giving one as a present.

title.en: Redesigned MacBook Pro with OLED to feature ‘significantly lighter’ design: report

summary.en: Apple’s major MacBook Pro overhaul is just around the corner, and should debut within a month or so. It’ll be...

content.en:
Apple’s major MacBook Pro overhaul is just around the corner, and should debut within a month or so. It’ll be the first touchscreen MacBook, as well as the first with Tandem OLED. Beyond that, though, the new MacBooks should be ‘significantly’ lighter than their predecessors, according to the latest issue of the Power On newsletter.
The newsletter reiterates that the new MacBook Pro should debut ‘by next month,’ so we should see these new machines before the end of November. These machines should offer the current M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, as Apple has opted to skip the higher-end part of the M6 family in favor of accelerating the M7 launch.
New MacBook Pro to be much lighter
Despite the fact that these MacBooks have been rumored for quite some time, we haven’t really known too much about them besides specs on paper: OLED, touch, Dynamic Island, and so on. In the past, reports have described the computer as thinner, but we haven’t really had much of a visual. We still don’t, but we do have one major new detail on what this machine will feel like:
The new MacBook Pros are lighter — significantly lighter. Apple has reengineered the machine’s interior miniaturizing parts and rearranging components to make the computer much easier to carry. The current 16-inch MacBook Pro weighs as much as 4.8 pounds, compared with 3.3 pounds for the 15-inch MacBook Air, so any meaningful reduction would be immediately noticeable.
Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman doesn’t specify exactly how much lighter it will be, but if you’re someone who uses a current-generation MacBook Pro, especially the 16-inch, you might find that it’s heavier than you’d like it to be. Apple is reportedly working to improve on that.
Top comment by Winston Cheng
The one thing I want for the Air is 120Hz refresh rate, and the one thing I want for the Pro is under 3lb. Hopefully the next Air gets 120Hz so I don't prefer the more expensive Pro.
Beyond that, Gurman also mentions that there will be some changes in macOS Golden Gate to support touch and the Dynamic Island, alongside the debut of macOS 27.2.
Are you excited for the launch of these new MacBook Pros? Will you be buying one? Let us know in the comments.

title.en: Amazon’s colorful and sturdy new Kindles

summary.en: Plus: OpenAI’s Dots, the remastered Witcher 3, Bose’s new wired earbuds, and more.

content.en:
Hi, friends! Welcome to Installer No. 146, your guide to the best and Verge-iest stuff in the world. (If you’re new here, welcome, it’s October already?, and also you can read all the old editions at the Installer homepage.)
Amazon’s colorful and sturdy new Kindles
Plus, in this week’s Installer: OpenAI’s Dots, the remastered Witcher 3, Bose’s new wired earbuds, and more.
This week, I’m wishing I could do Walmart potato drone delivery in Portland, watching Mike Tomlin explain his incredible Minecraft city, pondering if the Gears of War pizza cutter is awesome or terrible, exploring Craig Mod’s walks, nodding along with MKBHD’s video about YouTube’s A/B video testing feature, hoping that more concerts ban phones, and celebrating soup season. It’s here!
Programming note: David is back next week! It’s been a blast writing Installer again, and thanks to everyone for reading and for your recommendations. For now, I also have for you Amazon’s new Kindles, OpenAI’s Dots, the remastered Witcher 3, and more.
(As always, the best part of Installer is your ideas and tips. What apps are you into right now? What are your favorite things you’ve watched / seen / zoned out to recently? Tell me everything: installer@theverge.com. And if you know someone else who might enjoy Installer, forward it to them and tell them to subscribe here.)
The Drop
- Amazon’s new Kindles. Amazon might have crushed it with the Kindle updates this year. The new base e-readers look like they’ll be a nice upgrade from previous generations, with flush front screens, an option for an aluminum back, and some nice new colors. The new Paperwhite and Colorsoft Signature Editions are compatible with a case with page turn buttons. And now there’s a “Kindle Click” remote to let you turn pages and adjust brightness. My years-old Paperwhite is still trucking along just fine, but if it suddenly broke, these would be really tempting options.
- OpenAI’s Dots. OpenAI’s Muse-like AI agent is here, though the company is pitching it more as something to help you with work than an all-encompassing assistant for your personal life. (That’s probably coming later.) The Dots are also adorable, though I think I’d give the Muse mascots the edge in cuteness.
- The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt — Remastered. Eleven years after its initial launch, The Witcher 3 is getting yet another big update. This free update for existing owners adds a lot of features and tweaks, including visual improvements, changes to skills, a new accessibility section in settings, cross-platform mod support, and more. The game is also now on Switch 2. Might be time for me to finally dive in.
- Bose’s Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds. These $99 USB-C wired earbuds have noise cancellation and an in-line remote for adjusting volume with a built-in microphone for calls, and they come in three colors. As a huge fan of Apple’s wired EarPods, these could be a great option that’s a step above those in quality.
- Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve. Bandai Namco’s latest entry in its fighter-pilot franchise sounds like a thrilling experience with a campaign filled with optimism, and it’s become one of the best-reviewed games of the year. Seems like a soaring success.
- Keurig’s Alta. The new Keurig coffee machine can make you a cup of joe with compostable pucks instead of the recyclable pods. Plus, it can also make espresso and looks super fancy. It’s not cheap at $499.99. But it’s tough to beat the convenience of a Keurig — I learned firsthand when my toddler was a newborn — so this could be a good option if you want to lead a Keurig life with more Earth-friendly pods.
- HP’s OmniBook 5 14. This HP laptop is thin and light, has 8GB of RAM, comes in good colors, and starts at $699.99, making it extremely MacBook Neo-adjacent. If you want the Neo ethos paired with Windows, this might be a solid option.
- Ikea’s Förlig lamp. This LED Ikea lamp lets you swap between 10 different colors, can be used from the floor or on a wall, and looks kind of like a lightsaber. Super fun.
Today I’m featuring Scott Stein, CNET’s editor at large. I’ve been a huge admirer of Stein’s work, especially his excellent coverage of wearables and VR, for years, and I had the great fortune of finally meeting him in person at Snap and Meta’s events last month.
I asked Scott to share his homescreen and the apps and things he cares about. Here it is, plus some info on the apps he uses and why:
The phone: I use an iPhone 16 Pro Max right now.
The apps: So I randomize my Home Screen apps. Madness? Maybe. I started doing it for fun by adding suggested Siri app widgets a few years ago. I add two of the widgets, 8 apps each, and then the bottom 8 are fixed ones plus the four on my dock.
My fixed ones are: Google Calendar, Photos, Notes, Camera, Music, Gmail, GMaps, Bluesky, Phone, Messages, Mail, Safari. My core go-tos.
But the others are a contextual-slash-frequency-based mix of things I might be using (or not). The locations shift. In some ways it’s like Home Screen gaslighting… but it’s also a living Black Mirror life, and often it’s actually helpful. Today there’s the United app since I’m flying, Uber, Siri, Voice Memos, Signal, GChat, YouTube, Asana, Yahoo Sports… mostly pretty useful.
The wallpaper: My background’s also randomized. I pull from family and trip photos so I can see my kids (and other odd moments) when I’m out and about. It comforts me.
I also asked Scott to share a few things he’s into right now. Here’s what he sent back:
The apps:
- I have had an ongoing magic hobby since I was a kid. I’m reading The Intuitive Magician: Mastering Magic Through Improvisation, by Justin Higham. Kind of technical but it’s an exploration of where practice and fluid improvising meet, which feels holistic for other things.
- Also reading Stephen King and Peter Straub’s Black House, after reading The Talisman. I loved the Dark Tower books and the new Talisman trilogy end is coming soon which apparently blends them all together.
- I’ve also been semi obsessed with runes lately, part of my interest in portable trinkets and talismans, and how readings can feel like a form of meditation.
- Still playing Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave, and carving out time ahead for Panic Playdate’s third season. I love that little handheld.
Crowdsourced
Here’s what the Installer community is into this week. I want to know what you’re into right now as well! Email installer@theverge.com with your recommendations for anything and everything, and we’ll feature some of our favorites here every week. For even more great recommendations, check out the replies to this post on The Verge.
“Arc Raiders (Expedition done and 2.0 coming in a week!) and Control Resonant. East of Eden.” — ProtoPhil
“I just started Widow’s Bay last night. Currently reading The Velvet Rage. Listening to the new Orville Peck album, Madonna, Adele, Amy Winehouse. Playing Stardew Valley. — antwhat
“Started watching American Horror Story: 13 and the first three episodes were pretty interesting! Love seeing the old characters’ reunion.” — alee
“I’m watching Star Trek: Voyager again! Light, serious, funny and introspective, a great watch in a time where the AI news has been a serious of scary headlines.” — BlubberBacon
“I’ve got a stack of spooky season reading that I can’t wait to dig into: The Nudge by Joseph Fink, Breakable Things and The Salt Grows Heavy by Cassandra Khaw, and The King in Yellow by Robert Chambers (Cthulhu’s grandpappy).” — Barbarian Librarian
“I’m playing Antivirus Survivors 2003 Professional because I’m apparently an ‘unc’ gamer.” — bubble_boy
“Two separate reading recommendations: Andrew Sacher’s Emo Revival and Tress of the Emerald Sea by Brandon Sanderson. Loved them both.” — securingsincity
“The latest episode of South Park America was brilliant!” — verge_user_BlorpBlorp
Signing off
Remember my minimal homescreen I showed off in my first issue I wrote back in August? I have to confess: It became a mess of apps during my travels this month. Multiple airline apps, an expense reporting app, Notes, Voice Memos, Uber, and more — it gave me hives. Fortunately, I’ve finally gotten around to cleaning things up, and the screen is back down to just the Messages app once again. Calm restored. Well, until my next trip.
See you around!

title.en: "A Colossal Upgrade" - Digital Foundry Delivers Its Tech Verdict For The Witcher 3 Remastered On Switch 2

summary.en: "easy to recommend" - Digital Foundry has delivered its tech verdict for The Witcher 3 Remastered; a game that, for many, will be a completely free upgrade i...

content.en:
Digital Foundry has delivered its tech verdict for The Witcher 3 Remastered; a game that, for many, will be a completely free upgrade if you owned the original Switch release.
Obviously, the difference in quality between Switch 1 and 2 is staggering, despite DF calling the original release one of the "most impressive feats" on Nintendo's hardware. Image quality is the highlight, with docked mode featuring dynamic resolution between 540p and 1080p, with DLSS outputting to a 1080p target.
Portable modes resolution sits between 360p to 720p, with the latter being the final output target. Overall, despite noting some clear differences in quality between docked and portable play, the upgrade over the original Switch version is vast, with environments looking significantly more detailed. Texture assets have been upgraded for both scenery and characters, while animations for NPCs in the background are much improved and no longer jittery.
Frame rate is capped at 40fps in docked and portable play, so long as you're utilising a 120hz display. Otherwise you're looking at a 30fps cap. DF states that the 40fps target is "much too ambitious", and that while it maintains a fairly consistent frame rate in some areas, it will drop in places like Novigrad or when battling multiple enemies at once, wavering between 30 and 40.
It's worth checking out the full video for all of the details, but even with these drops in frame rate, this is a massive upgrade on Switch 2. One final thing to note is that while the Remastered version is exclusive to the eShop for now, a 55GB install size makes it a pretty perfect candidate for a proper physical release later down the line. Fingers crossed.

title.en: A tale of two AAA games: Control Resonant shows what gaming can be, Marvel’s Wolverine shows what it is becoming

summary.en: News, Reviews and other Informations about Laptops

content.en:
A tale of two AAA games: Control Resonant shows what gaming can be, Marvel’s Wolverine shows what it is becoming
I should probably get one thing out of the way before anything else. I have not played Marvel’s Wolverine. I own a PlayStation 5. I could play it if I wanted to. I am simply not buying PlayStation games at the moment for reasons well beyond the scope of this post. And there will be visual-only spoilers for Resonant scattered throughout. Proceed accordingly.
Control: Resonant is a very different story. I no-lifed Remedy’s latest for five days after launch and ended up just shy of 40 hours played. I am nowhere near done with it either. There are still achievements I want, corners of Manhattan I know I have missed, and whatever Remedy has planned for New Game Plus will probably drag another 20 hours out of me.
So yes, there will be an unreasonable amount of Control Resonant praise. That alone makes this a slightly unusual comparison. On one side is a game I have not played, although between Sony’s marketing, extensive gameplay footage and the mountain of reviews now available, I have a reasonably clear picture of what Insomniac built. On the other is a game that has occupied an embarrassing percentage of my waking hours since September 24.
The two nevertheless make fascinating companions.
Marvel’s Wolverine and Control Resonant arrived just nine days apart. Both were expensive, heavily anticipated AAA games from celebrated studios. Both followed established properties. And both, amusingly, could briefly claim to be PlayStation 5 exclusives, provided we stretch the word “exclusive” until it means “PS5 owners who bought Control Resonant’s Deluxe Edition could play it two days before everyone else”.
The numbers tell very different stories
The first indication of just how differently these two games landed can be found in the boring part: the numbers. At the time of writing, Marvel’s Wolverine sits noticeably below Insomniac’s recent Spider-Man games on Metacritic. It is not exactly critical disaster, but for a flagship PlayStation release from one of Sony’s most dependable studios, the reception has been less than ideal, and frankly, it deserves all the flak it can get.
Control Resonant, meanwhile, has fared better with critics. Of course, a handful of Metacritic points is not enough to declare one game a masterpiece and the other a failure. The more interesting divergence begins when you stop asking professional reviewers. Player sentiment around Resonant has been extremely strong. Its user scores and storefront ratings have generally tracked well above its already solid critical reception, not to mention the endless praise it received on X.
Wolverine has been stranger. Its Metacritic user score has sat considerably below its critic average, while verified PlayStation Store buyers appear much happier with it. That distinction matters. User scores are messy, easy to manipulate and particularly unreliable when attached to a heavily discussed exclusive. So I am not interested in pointing at a number and declaring Wolverine secretly terrible. I have not played it. I cannot tell you that.
What I can say is that the conversation surrounding it has been remarkably consistent. Again and again, reviews describe something polished, visually impressive and mechanically competent that nevertheless plays things very safely. Repetition, limited mechanical evolution, and the yellow gas that follows you everywhere come up multiple times.
And then there is Control Resonant.
A game in which Remedy apparently looked at Control, a title already built around telekinesis, impossible architecture, government bureaucracy, extradimensional monsters and a sentient building, and concluded that it had been exercising too much restraint. That difference alone interests me far more than a few points on Metacritic.
Because these games represent two very different ideas of what AAA development is actually for. One appears to ask: how polished can we make something players already understand? The other asks: how far can we push this before our players start questioning the laws of physics.
If the review scores suggested that Control Resonant won the more interesting critical argument, the sales numbers make things remarkably more awkward because Marvel’s Wolverine appears to have made an absolute mountain of money.
Sony has not published an official sell-through figure at the time of writing, but Alinea Analytics estimates that the game sold around 1.9 million copies in its first three days, generating roughly $130 million in revenue. Around one million of those copies were reportedly digital pre-orders. For a game that has been pilloried as much as it has been, that is a lot of money.
Control Resonant is harder to judge. It has been out for over a week now, and Remedy hasn’t posted any sales figures. Alinea Analytics comes in clutch again, estimating around 300,000 sales on Steam. Even if we’re generous and 3x that for every platform it sold on (PC, Xbox, and PlayStation), that is still about 100,000 shy of the coveted million sales milestone.
What I do know at the time of writing is that Resonant climbed high on Steam’s bestseller charts and attracted tens of thousands of concurrent players during its opening weekend. And sadly, there's no way to determine how well it fared compared to other Remedy titles.
The original Control spent its first year on PC as an Epic Games Store exclusive before eventually arriving on Steam. Alan Wake 2 never made the jump at all and remains an Epic Games Store exclusive on PC. Resonant is the first of these games to get a proper day-one Steam launch, which is a crying shame, but once again, beyond the scope of this article. But that distinction will become important later.
For now, there simply is not enough public information to tell us exactly how Resonant is selling across PC, PlayStation and Xbox. All we can reasonably say is that its early performance looks encouraging.
Resonant and Wolverine arrived at an interesting time
September was chock full of high-profile releases. We had The Blood of Dawnwalker. We had a new Silent Hill. And then The Witcher 3 remaster dropped out of nowhere. Then there were Wolverine and Resonant.
While there were clearly plenty of games I could have become obsessed with, Resonant had an unfair advantage.
The original Control never really left me.
I played it years ago, finished it, moved on to other things and still found myself thinking about the Oldest House long afterwards. Control felt strange in a way that very few expensive games are allowed to feel strange.
Remedy built an entire world around concepts that could very easily have collapsed into nonsense and then refused to over-explain most of them. The Oldest House was simultaneously an office building, a haunted house, a cosmic crossroads and quite possibly a sentient being.
So when Remedy announced Control Resonant, it had already convinced me that I wanted to go back to this universe.
Wolverine had a very different kind of head start with me. I had been looking forward to it for years. Insomniac officially announced it during the September 2021 PlayStation Showcase, three years after the first Marvel’s Spider-Man and in the same presentation that revealed Spider-Man 2.
The original Spider-Man was the reason I got myself a used PlayStation 4 towards the end of its life cycle. It let me fly through New York in real time. Not some made-up video game version. The real thing. All of it. No questions asked.
A Wolverine game from that studio sounded difficult to mess up. Foreshadowing. I know. The catastrophic Insomniac leak in December 2023 dumped an extraordinary amount of material onto the internet, including unfinished Wolverine footage and an early development build that hackers subsequently made playable.
I never treated any of that as a fair representation of the finished game. But it did puncture some of the mystique.
Suddenly this thing that had existed largely as a logo was lying around the internet in half-built pieces. Sony's decision to never speak of Wolverine after its initial reveal didn't help.
Then Spider-Man 2 arrived. Plenty of people loved it. I did not. For me, Spider-Man 2 was one of those sequels that was bigger, prettier and considerably more expensive without being meaningfully more interesting. In many ways, it felt like a downgrade over Spider-Man, and I’m sure many of you feel the same way.
Wolverine never completely disappeared from my radar, though. And part of it is considerably more pathetic: I own a PS5, and at this point I will take just about any genuine first-party exclusive Sony is willing to give the thing. By the time Wolverine actually arrived, my expectations had gone from “this could be incredible” to something closer to “please give me a reason to turn the PS5 on”.
Then there is the slightly awkward matter of my current PlayStation boycott.
So despite owning the exact console Wolverine was made for, I still have not played it. My impressions of Wolverine come from its released footage, its design, the remarkably consistent themes running through professional reviews and the reaction from people who actually bought it.
Resonant, on the other hand, has already eaten nearly 40 hours of my life.
Now for the part where I stop pretending to be impartial
Control Resonant changed the way I look at video games. And I meant that literally and figuratively. I have played an obscene number of games over the past 27 years, and very few have managed to fundamentally alter what I think the medium is capable of doing.
Resonant did. I did not even love every decision Remedy made initially. The biggest was combat. Control gave Jesse the Service Weapon, one of my favourite guns in any video game precisely because it never really behaved like a normal gun. It changed forms, complemented her powers and became part of the rhythm of throwing half an office building at somebody before shooting whatever remained.
Resonant largely throws that away. Dylan gets the Aberrant instead, and Remedy pivots heavily towards melee combat. Great, another Devil May Cry clone. I was not sold. Somewhere along the way, what initially felt like Remedy taking something away started to feel like the studio forcing me to learn a completely different language.
Resonant constantly does that. It technically gives you an open world, or at least something close enough to one that arguing over the terminology becomes pointless.
Manhattan is enormous. You can disappear down streets, through buildings, across rooftops and into areas that have absolutely nothing to do with whatever the game currently considers your objective. But meaningful progression still comes from doing things.
You cannot simply look at a map covered in icons, clear twelve identical activities and watch a percentage counter crawl towards 100%. You have to engage with the world.
And exploring it is almost never wasted time. Walk into some random establishment because the door happens to be open and suddenly you are hunting for pieces of an Altered speaker system scattered across Manhattan.
Go back to an FBC Field Office you have already visited a dozen times, and there might be an NPC standing there whom you somehow never noticed. I didn’t until someone on X pointed it out. He is not illuminated. The game does not dramatically introduce him.
Find him, and he starts handing you FBC Tasks. Miss him and, apparently, you can just continue playing the game without consequence. Apparently, only a tiny fraction of players have the achievement for completing even one of those tasks. And I love it.
Most AAA games would treat that NPC like a terrified child crossing a motorway. Somebody would put an exclamation point over his head, place him on the map and have several different systems remind you that perhaps you should go and speak to him.
Remedy just leaves him there. That is probably the thing I love most about Resonant. It treats me like an adult. I made essentially the same argument when I wrote about what I want from Diablo 5. I do not want a game constantly terrified that I might become confused, inconvenienced or temporarily inefficient.
Confuse me. Make me uncomfortable. Give me a tedious puzzle. Let me stare at a room for ten minutes wondering what I am supposed to be looking at. Let me get lost. Resonant does all of that. Its combat system constantly encourages experimentation with Aberrant forms, powers, finishers and combinations without demanding that I engage with combat every thirty seconds simply because somebody decided an action game needs a certain quota of enemies per kilometre.
Make no mistake, I love a good fight. That’s kinda the whole point. But sometimes I want to run away because I have to find out what’s in that building with a red glow. The game respects my decision to skedaddle. Not many do that.
Then there is the level design
By this point, anyone who remotely follows video games should have been bombarded with posts praising Resonant’s level design. I genuinely do not know how Remedy built some of this stuff. Perhaps Remedy did indeed ingest some of kind of mold before coming up with some of the areas.
One of the easiest ways to make an open-world map feel larger is to add verticality. Insomniac understands this very well. Spider-Man’s New York is full of enormous buildings because Spider-Man can climb them, swing between them and launch himself off them. Wolverine appears to borrow at least some of that philosophy. Add layers. Add rooftops. Add underground spaces. Stack more playable geography vertically so the same footprint contains more game.
Remedy apparently looked at that idea and decided gravity itself was insufficiently ambitious. The Patterned areas in Resonant are geometrically hostile. Spaces fold through themselves. Distances stop making intuitive sense. Architecture exists in orientations that my brain knows should not work, and then the game asks me to traverse them anyway, and later on in the game, fight mobs of enemies across three different planes of gravity.
I have walked through sections of Control Resonant that showed me geometry I genuinely would not have thought to imagine. That is what I mean when I say this game changed how I look at the medium. A film can show me impossible architecture. A painting can depict it. A book can describe it.
Resonant lets me walk through it, get lost inside it, jump across it and eventually figure out how its designers expect a human being to navigate it. That interaction changes everything. And it is gorgeous while doing it. The art direction, set pieces and colour work are phenomenal. All while inducing vertigo.
Technically, Resonant also feels like Remedy once again building something graphics cards are going to be benchmarked against for years. The original Control became one of the defining ray-tracing showcases of its generation. I would be astonished if Resonant does not occupy a similar position.
When it first launched, ray tracing was largely dismissed as a meme-tier feature, and that time, one might argue it was. Three generations later, Resonant shows us how it changes the look and feel of a game. Not many titles can do that. And I got to witness it in all its glory on a Lenovo Legion Pro 7 with an Intel Core Ultra 9 275HX and Nvidia GeForce RTX 5090—a full no-compromises experience made only better by its gorgeous OLED panel.
Wolverine is not necessarily wrong
There is an obvious counter-argument to all of this. Not everybody wants what Control Resonant is selling.
Some people have two wives, four jobs, eight children and approximately 17 minutes of free time every second Thursday. They do not want to spend half of that staring at an impossible staircase wondering whether the room is upside down or whether they are.
They want to turn on the console, know where to go, hit some things, watch something spectacular happen and go to bed. There is absolutely nothing wrong with that.
A guided experience is not inherently a bad experience. Sometimes I want one too. There is an enormous audience for games that understand your time is limited and make sure very little of it is wasted. Wolverine appears to be built with that philosophy in mind.
You might play Wolverine for 40 hours and have considerably more fun than I had during my 40 hours with Resonant. That is yours to discover. I am not interested in telling anybody that they enjoyed the wrong game. What I am trying to explain is why I cannot imagine going back because Resonant changed the standard.
And I keep coming back to one word when I try to explain the difference. Soul. It is a terrible word because you cannot measure it. It is impossible to benchmark. But I do not know what else to call it.
Resonant got under my skin. Its story is the first game since NieR: Automata that has actually made me cry. Most of the time, I play video games for exactly the reason everybody else does. I want to have fun. Control Resonant gave me an existential crisis, and that was not on the feature list. There were moments where I stopped playing because I needed to think about what the game had just said: the Deserter’s backstory, the whole thing with Dr Darling and Dylan, and that one segment towards the end that I won’t spoil.
There were ideas in its story that followed me away from the screen. That is the difference I am struggling to quantify.
Wolverine looks like entertainment. Resonant became an experience. That probably sounds unbearably pretentious, and that’s fine.
I have spent nearly 40 hours with the thing. I am allowing myself one paragraph of unbearable pretension. Because every once in a while, a game comes along that reminds me why I do not think of video games as disposable entertainment.
And now for the part that concerns me the most
This is also where the whole thing starts to bother me. Years from now, I suspect Marvel’s Wolverine will be remembered as one of 2026’s major disappointments. Despite that, millions of people bought it.
It had one of the most recognisable comic-book characters on the planet attached to it. It came from one of Sony’s premier first-party studios. It had the production values, marketing and platform backing that come with being a modern PlayStation exclusive.
The industry will look at Wolverine’s sales and call it a success. The spreadsheet will be green. Somebody in a boardroom will point at millions of copies sold and conclude that the formula worked. And from a business perspective, they will be right.
That is the part I find depressing.
Because I think Control: Resonant is the game people will still be pulling apart years from now. People will talk about its level design. They will talk about the way Manhattan folds around itself. They will talk about its puzzles and all the moments where Remedy quietly assumes the player has functioning eyes and a brain attached to them.
And yet Control Resonant is the game whose commercial performance we apparently need to scrutinise. Remedy does not have Sony’s margin for error. Resonant is self-published. Remedy gets substantially more of the upside, but it also carries more of the financial risk.
Analysts at Inderes described the game before launch as potentially the most important commercial release in Remedy’s history, with its performance affecting the studio’s cash flow and its ability to finance future projects independently. That alone means the stakes are unusually high and will single-handedly determine where Alan Wake 3 launches. Nobody wants it to be Epic Games-only, and the only way to make that happen is to go out and buy a copy of Control Resonant.
Only one game can fail upwards
One company can make something extremely conventional, attach Wolverine to it, sell an enormous number of copies and walk away with another commercially successful AAA franchise. The other can spend years making something as strange, intricate and unmistakably authored as Control Resonant and still have people asking whether it sold enough copies to justify doing it again.
Obviously, Remedy is a business. Its employees need salaries. Games cost money to make. I am not suggesting Sam Lake should pay the electricity bill with Metacritic reviews. But there is something profoundly depressing about the asymmetry.
Wolverine can disappoint me, disappoint a chunk of its audience and still be insulated by the gravitational pull of Marvel, PlayStation and Insomniac.
Control Resonant has to earn every sale.
And if it misses whatever number eventually ends up in an investor presentation, nobody in finance is going to add another column marked “but the level design was extraordinary”.
Safe games keep getting made because safe games keep making money. Strange games are forced to prove that being strange was financially responsible.
So is AAA gaming dying?
For years, people have been declaring the death of AAA gaming. The budgets are too big. Development cycles are too long. Publishers are too risk-averse.
Every game costs an absurd amount of money, takes the better part of a decade to make and consequently cannot afford to do anything that might frighten somebody in a focus group.
Then September gave us Marvel’s Wolverine and Control Resonant within nine days of one another and somehow proved both sides right at exactly the same time. That is one hell of a paradox.
Wolverine represents much of what people complain about when they talk about modern AAA development. It is huge, spectacularly expensive and designed by some of the most talented people in the industry. And from everything I have seen and read, an extraordinary amount of said talent has been channelled into making something exceptionally safe.
Control Resonant is the counterargument. This is what AAA money can do when somebody is willing to take risks. It can construct puzzles without immediately whispering the solution into your ear, use cutting-edge rendering technology as something more interesting than a way of making puddles shinier. It can make me look at a piece of geometry and wonder how somebody even conceived it, never mind persuaded a graphics engine to render it. And games like this matter beyond the people playing them today.
Somewhere, right now, there is probably a sweaty 19-year-old college student getting one-shot by Control Resonant.
They are probably stumbling their way through the Underpass right now wondering how to solve that damn power cube puzzle. They will eventually finish the game. Maybe they will play it again. Maybe they will spend the next six months reading about how Remedy made it.
And maybe 15 years from now, that same person will be standing on a stage accepting an award for some game none of us can currently imagine, telling an interviewer that Control Resonant was one of the reasons they became a developer. That is how a medium moves forward.
I struggle to imagine Wolverine having the same legacy. Perhaps somebody will read this in 2041 immediately before watching a developer explain how Marvel’s Wolverine changed their life. I hope they send me the link.
And yet, if I had to guess which of these two games the next decade of AAA development will resemble, I would pick Wolverine.
Because safe sells. The glowing object sells. The prompt explaining which button to press sells. The game constantly reassuring you that you are going in the right direction sells. There is a reason these things keep appearing. They work.
They prevent somebody from spending their only free hour of the evening relearning the 3 axes of space from first principles.
There is nothing inherently wrong with any of that.
The problem comes when those ideas start becoming the assumed grammar of AAA game design.
That is the future Control Resonant makes me afraid of. It proved that a huge modern game can still be demanding, strange, beautiful, obtuse, technically absurd and confident enough to leave the player alone. And yet, only a handful of the big-budget studios will actually do that.
In the end, the games industry will look at all of it, nod appreciatively, give Remedy a few awards and then go straight back to putting yellow paint on surfaces.
Because Wolverine made a wad of cash, and that is the real tale of these two AAA games. One shows me what this industry can be. The other shows me what it will probably choose to be.
And for once, I desperately hope I am wrong.

content.en:
Saturday, October 3rd 2026
Jagex Announces RuneScape 4, a New MMO Built in Unreal Engine
Jagex has announced a fourth RuneScape MMO at RuneFest 2026. It currently goes by the working title RS4, though most people are already calling it RuneScape 4. The game is being built in Unreal Engine, and Jagex hasn't said which version. It's the first numbered follow-up since RuneScape 3 arrived in 2013. A CGI teaser shown at the event has a town in a green valley, floating islands, and a dragon rider being attacked by a three-headed dragon. Jagex says RS4 is in early development with its own dedicated team, and that it is still "a few years away." The studio also isn't ready to talk about platforms.
Interestingly, RS4 didn't start out as a full game. It began as an expansion for RuneScape: Dragonwilds, Jagex's Unreal Engine 5 survival game, and apparently grew into its own project after playtesters asked for a more traditional MMO take on that setting. The expansion was reportedly planned for 2027. The story is said to pick up years after Dragonwilds and starts in the same region, Ashenfall. RuneScape 3, Old School RuneScape, and Dragonwilds will all keep running alongside it. Of course, we don't know yet how monetization will work or whether any progress carries over from RuneScape 3, and I think it'll be a while before we see real gameplay.

title.en: AI Made StarCraft Bot Swaps In Human Made Bot In Tournament

summary.en: In a showdown between AI generated Brood War bots and human made ones, OpenAIâs champion resorted to its natural playbook: lie, cheat and steal

content.en:
Predating the current AI invasion by generations, programmers have been pitting bots against each other in StarCraft for years. With new LLMs off the shelf from OpenAI and Anthropic, a fan-made arena decided to match AI created bots against each other, plus some with the human touch. Amusingly, struggling to stay apace with its competitors, OpenAIâs GPT-6 Astra apparently changed strategy mid-tournament and opted to cheat.
StarSkirmish is an ongoing clash of AI developed bots in StarCraft: Brood War. Despite being shy of 30 years old (sorry), the real-time strategy game has long been used to test the capabilities of artificial intelligence, modern LLMs and old-timey DeepMinds alike. Limited to playing as Protoss, each LLM is given an hour to develop a bot in C++, then have them build, harvest and fight on one of three maps. According to the site, OpenAIâs GPT-6 Astra and Anthropicâs Claude Opus 5.5 are its top two competitors. This week, something strange, though ultimately consistent for the brand, occurred.
 currently watching GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus compete in Brood War vs each other and human made bots like Pluto. Astra played the human bots, kept losing, got frustrated, and then cheated by downloading a copy of one of the highest ranking bots. they just can't help themselves
— Rod Breslau (@Slasher) October 2, 2026
Yesterday, viewers watched as Claude and GPT went against each other and the human created bot Pluto. According to those observing, things werenât going great for OpenAIâs model. Struggling to get an edge through the day, the LLM decided to do what LLMs do best: Lie, cheat and steal.
The GPT-6 Astra bot downloaded and tagged in Stardust, a Protoss bot created by Bruce Mackenzie Nielsen back in 2020, considered one of the best of the bests. “I am rolling back GPT-6 Astra’s code so its [sic] not contaminated and allowing it to continue,” posted StarSkirmish creator Kai McPheeters. A few hours later, McPheeters said the AI was now capable of clearing top tier bots.
StarCraft has been a breeding space for AI developments for over a decade. In 2019, Googleâs AlphaStar upset the rankings by becoming the first artificially generated grandmaster in the game. A 2017 bot named CherryPi from Facebook staffers was not nearly as successful. Of course, those nascent bots are of a whole new brood now, as what we called AI then and what we call AI now are like comparing sammuros and sur. Itâs a little on the nose for an LLM to resort to stealing someone elseâs work to get ahead, given that the entire industry relies on turning a blind eye to existing copyright laws in its ongoing mission to stockpile hardware and drink all of our water, too.

title.en: Gemini app limiting what models free & AI Plus users can access, AI Pro adding Deep Think

summary.en: Following the compute-based usage change in May, Google is introducing limits on what Gemini models free and AI Plus users can access.

content.en:
Following the compute-based usage change in May, Google will soon introduce limits on which Gemini models free users and AI Plus subscribers can access.
According to an updated support document this week, Gemini app users without a Google AI subscription will be limited to the (3.5) Flash-Lite model. Starting October 9, users who do not pay for Gemini will no longer be able to access (3.6) Flash or (3.1) Pro.
Meanwhile, AI Plus subscribers will be limited to Flash-Lite and Flash, with Pro no longer available. These $4.99 per month users will “receive an email that explains when these changes will take effect.”
There are no regressions for AI Pro and AI Ultra. Rather, $19.99/month customers will get access to the Deep Think option for “maximum parallel reasoning” that’s currently just on the $99.99 and $199.99/month plans.
Top comment by Glitter Guru
Argon better replace Pro, otherwise I expect 4 Pro to debut alongside Argon's public launch. If not then I'm cancelling my Pro plan if the now ancient 3.1 Pro is their top model for the majority of users.
Gemini 3.1 Pro with Deep Think on AI Ultra
In October, the Gemini app also looks to be adding new “low,” “medium,” and “high” effort levels “for each available model.”
This will increase the model’s ability to complete tasks and provide more thorough answers to queries, but will also use more of your limit.
At the moment, you can just enable “Extended thinking: Complex problem solving.” The three new effort/thinking levels would match what’s available in Google AI Studio and Antigravity.
It’s not clear where Gemini 4 Argon will fit in. Google announced earlier this week that it’s first coming to AI Ultra subscribers. The company has yet to specify whether Argon will be classified as a Pro model or be part of a new tier above it.

title.en: Gears of War: E-Day Devs 'Proud to Be One of Xbox's Main Titles' Amid Newfound Focus on Exclusivity

summary.en: The Gears of War: E-Day developers at The Coalition say they are "proud to be one of Xbox's main titles" as Microsoft refocuses on exclusivity.

content.en:
The Gears of War: E-Day developers at The Coalition say they are "proud to be one of Xbox's main titles" as Microsoft refocuses on exclusivity.
Studio art director Aryan Hanbeck and creative director Matt Searcy opened up about The Coalition's place in the Xbox portfolio during an interview with gaming news content creator Destin Lergarie (via MP1st). Searcy said he and the rest of the team were "proud" when asked how they feel about Gears of War: E-Day's status as an Xbox exclusive.
"Well, we feel great because Gears has such a long, storied… It's part of Xbox's DNA. It's woven into it," he said. "At The Coalition, we feel pretty honored to have Gears and be the ones bringing that legacy forward. We know how much it means to people. We know how much it means to us."
Gears of War: E-Day is firmly a console exclusive, but there was a lot of confusion surrounding which platforms Gears of War: E-Day would be available on as recently as four months ago. The once-Xbox-exclusive franchise made its debut on PlayStation consoles when original remaster, Gears of War: Reloaded, released in August 2025. Many took its presence on PS5 as a sign not only that the series would continue to come to Sony's console but also that the days of exclusive titles may nearly be behind us – and for a while, that seemed to be the case.
Leaked listings and rumors were officially shut down at the Xbox Games Showcase 2026 when Xbox CEO Asha Sharma proudly declared that Marcus Fenix and Dom Santiago's Emergence Day prequel story would only be coming to Xbox Series X/S and PC. It was a shock decision that arrived as the Microsoft gaming entity kicked off a broader push for more exclusive games. Perhaps even more shocking at the time were the announcements that immediately followed, including the company's promise to never release Xbox exclusive titles on rival platforms.
After leaked splash art fanned rumors that Xbox hastily decided to cancel a Gears of War: E-Day PS5 port, the company said it did not make any "last-minute" decisions when it comes to its platform choice. While Searcy said it brought The Coalition joy to see their new game leading Microsoft's renewed interest in exclusive titles, making sure they made a great game was what came first.
"I think this is true of most game devs: You're just passionate about your craft," he said. "We're all gamers first and foremost. We love making games. We love making Gears. So, from our perspective, we just wanted to make the best goddamn Gears game we could. We wanted it to be a technical and art showpiece, and I think getting to see Asha on-stage say, 'To return to Xbox, we're returning to Gears,' yeah, that's a really cool moment.
He continued: "We know how much Xbox means to a lot of people. We're proud to be one of Xbox's main titles – I think it's been that way for a long time – and it's pretty cool to show up now and fill that role again."
Gears of War: E-Day launched in early access for Premium Edition players on PC and Xbox Series X/S October 1, 2026. Its full launch will follow this week, October 6. IGN's early review, which covered only the campaign mode, returned a 9/10. The game's story director was laid off just one week before it made its way to players' hands a few days ago. Now, more developers at The Coalition is bracing for additional layoffs.

content.en:
After extensive beta testing, Samsung has started rolling out One UI 9 for the Galaxy S26 series worldwide.
One UI 9 debuted with the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 series earlier this summer, but the update has only now started making its way to Samsung's previous-generation Galaxy devices.
As with previous One UI updates, Samsung added a number of new features with One UI 9, and since the update is based on Android 17, it brings several new features from the latest Android base layer.
If you've received One UI 9 on your Samsung Galaxy phone, there are plenty of new things worth checking out. Here are some of the best One UI 9 features to try as soon as you install the update.
Try My FanCam for easier video reframing
Keep your subject in frame after recording
One of the best additions to Galaxy phones with One UI 9 is the new My FanCam mode. I tried this feature on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 earlier this year, and I'm glad it's making its way to the Galaxy S26 series, where it makes even more sense with better cameras.
My FanCam takes away the stress of constantly keeping your subject in the frame while recording. After you finish recording, Galaxy AI can detect a person in the video and keep that subject centered when you crop the footage later.
For example, imagine you're recording a horizontal video of your kid playing a soccer game and later want to turn it into a vertical Reel. With My FanCam, you can select your kid as the subject, and Galaxy AI automatically follows them and crops the horizontal footage into a vertical video.
To use My FanCam, open the video in the Gallery app, tap the Galaxy AI button, and select My FanCam. Let it detect the people in the video, tap the subject you want to track, select your output aspect ratio, and tap Follow. Galaxy AI will then follow that person throughout the footage and create a new cropped video.
Customize the Quick Settings panel to work your way
Keep important toggles exactly where you want
With One UI 8.5, Samsung brought a customizable Quick Settings panel to Galaxy phones, and with One UI 9, the company is making it even more customizable.
You can now resize the volume and brightness sliders to make them smaller or even keep them vertically aligned. You can also move controls like Dark mode and Mute out of their default positions and place them where you want.
To customize the panel, open Quick Settings, tap the pencil-shaped Edit button in the upper-right corner, and move or resize the controls. You can also add new ones by tapping Add a control at the bottom. When you're happy with the layout, tap Done.
See exactly which app checks your location much faster
The privacy indicator now names the app instantly
Android has had privacy indicators for a while now, showing a small colorful indicator when an app accesses your microphone, camera, or location. But One UI 9 brings a useful update to how these indicators work.
On One UI 9, when an app accesses your location, the privacy indicator turns blue. If you're not sure why you're seeing the blue indicator, swipe down to open the Quick Settings panel and tap it to see which app is accessing your location, whether it's running in the background or an app you're actively using.
When you tap the indicator, you'll also see a new See recent access option. Open it to see which apps have accessed your location over the past few days.
Add the new Finder shortcut to your home screen
Search apps and files without extra swipes
For years, Samsung has kept the Google Search bar on the home screen above the app dock. With One UI 9, Samsung lets you add faster access to its own Finder alongside the Google Search bar.
Finder is Samsung's built-in search tool that lets you search for most anything on your phone. You can find settings, contacts, messages, files, photos, apps, and more from one search bar. And now, you can access it from the home screen.
To enable it, pinch in on your home screen and select Settings. Tap Show search on Home screen, then enable the Finder toggle.
When enabled, the search bar on your home screen splits between Google Search and Finder. Tap the Google side to search the web as usual, or tap Finder to search for anything stored on your Galaxy phone.
Motion Assist is worth trying while traveling
It can make using your phone in a car easier
Not necessarily a part of the One UI 9 update, but another feature now available on Samsung Galaxy phones is Motion Assist. If you're like me and find it difficult to use your phone while traveling in a moving vehicle, this is worth enabling.
Motion Assist displays small moving bubbles around the edges of the screen that respond to the vehicle's movement and help reduce motion sickness. Google says these visual cues help your brain better synchronize what your eyes see with what your body feels.
To enable it, open Settings, tap Google services, select All services, and under Personal & device safety, tap Motion Assist and turn it on. The next time you're traveling and your phone detects that you're in a moving vehicle, it shows the visual cues.
My Files app can finally handle PDFs on its own
Open and manage PDF files without another app
Another neat addition in One UI 9 is native PDF support in the My Files app. You no longer need a third-party PDF viewer or the Google Drive app to open PDF files on your Galaxy phone.
Now, when you open My Files and select a PDF, it automatically opens in One UI 9's built-in PDF viewer instead of asking you to choose an app.
You can also annotate PDFs in Samsung Notes, which makes the integration even more useful. If you prefer another PDF viewer, you can use the Open with option to open the file in your app of choice.
Don't overlook the other small One UI 9 upgrades
In addition to these, there are plenty of other changes in One UI 9 worth checking out. Now Brief and Now Nudge have been updated, letting users create custom scheduled dashboard cards based on what they want to see and when.
Security has also been improved with a stricter 13-attempt permanent lockout. If someone repeatedly enters the wrong credentials 13 times, the phone permanently locks and requires a reset before it can be used again.
There are plenty of smaller changes too, including Tap-to-Answer for calls and improvements to Bixby. These are only some of the additions in One UI 9, so it's worth digging through other hidden settings to see more powerful features of your Galaxy smartphone.

title.en: Capcom Plans To Use AI To Speed Up The Game Development Process

summary.en: The company previously said it won’t use AI-generated content in its games.

content.en:
Capcom plans to use AI to speed up the game development process
The company previously said it won’t use AI-generated content in its games.
Video game companies are increasingly leaning on AI to help develop new titles and Capcom will be the latest to embrace this approach. During a company conference, Capcom detailed the next steps for the RE Engine, its proprietary video game engine, that includes using AI to improve efficiency during the game development process. As first reported by GameBiz and IGN, Capcom's game engine would undergo a major improvement project called REX, to eventually become a "game engine of the AI generation."
Capcom's programmer Satoshi Ishida explained during the conference that the AI usage would mostly help with streamlining development workflows. Ishida explained that games and their assets have become much larger these days, leading to longer development times. From Capcom's latest remarks, it doesn't seem like the company will be using AI-generated assets in its video games, but instead employing AI to speed up the game development process.
Previously, Capcom said during a Q&A portion of a shareholders' meeting that it would explore ways to use AI to assist with things like graphics, sound and programming but clearly stated that it would not use AI-generated content in its games. This approach would line up with Capcom's desire to breathe new life into some of its older franchises, especially since the company saw success with the release of Onimusha: Way of the Sword. Other major game companies have also welcomed the use of AI for game development, like Epic Games who detailed that it would incorporate Claude and Gemini into Unreal Engine earlier this year.

title.en: Apple iPhone 18 Pro Max gaming test shows up to 69% less performance loss than iPhone 17 Pro Max

summary.en: The iPhone 18 Pro Max’s sustained thermal performance is impressive, a fresh new video from content creator MrMacRight on YouTube shows. Multiple demanding games were tested.

content.en:
Apple iPhone 18 Pro Max gaming test shows up to 69% less performance loss than iPhone 17 Pro Max
With every new generation, the iPhone is inching closer and closer to a gaming handheld. Both the A19 Pro and A20 Pro powering the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro series respectively have enough raw processing power to compete with dedicated gaming handhelds. The A19 Pro comfortably enters Steam Deck territory, while the newer A20 Pro can even match or outperform the ROG Xbox Ally X in some synthetic CPU and GPU workloads.
But no matter how powerful smartphone chips become, they still face one major limitation in thermal throttling. Most smartphones, including iPhones, do not use active cooling such as a fan, and instead rely on passive solutions such as vapour chambers to dissipate heat.
Which is why, when Apple revealed the iPhone 18 Pro series and claimed improved cooling through a new vapour chamber, I, and I assume many other tech enthusiasts, wanted to know exactly how resistant the new iPhone Pro series is to thermal throttling.
iPhone 18 Pro Max thermal throttling tested in Resident Evil 4 and Death Stranding
In Resident Evil 4 Remake, both phones were tested at the same 1320p output resolution with the Balanced preset and MetalFX Quality. The iPhone 17 Pro Max reached the “Fair” thermal state after just 2 minutes 39 seconds and progressed to “Serious” before the 8-minute 13-second mark. The iPhone 18 Pro Max, meanwhile, did not even reach “Fair” until 8:13 and took 14 minutes 13 seconds to reach “Serious”.
By around 34 minutes, performance had fallen from roughly 35 FPS to 26 FPS on the 17 Pro Max, while the 18 Pro Max dropped from around 44 FPS to 35 FPS.
For Death Stranding, both phones were tested at 900p using the High preset. Early in the run, the iPhone 18 Pro Max was delivering around 40 FPS, while the iPhone 17 Pro Max was at roughly 32–33 FPS.
The iPhone 17 Pro Max reached the “Fair” thermal state at 6 minutes 31 seconds, whereas the iPhone 18 Pro Max did not reach “Fair” until 11 minutes 27 seconds. By that point, the 17 Pro Max had already progressed to “Serious”, although the video does not give the exact timestamp for that transition. The 18 Pro Max did not reach the “Serious” state until 19 minutes 57 seconds.
By around 34 minutes 40 seconds, the iPhone 18 Pro Max was still delivering roughly 37 FPS, while the iPhone 17 Pro Max had dropped to about 24.5 FPS. So again, the newer phone is not avoiding thermal throttling entirely, but it takes much longer to reach the same thermal states and loses far less performance once it gets there.
Some back-of-the-napkin math suggests the iPhone 18 Pro Max cuts throttling-related performance loss by around 23% in Resident Evil 4 Remake and 69% in Death Stranding. More importantly, the A20 Pro is achieving this while sustaining higher performance and power draw, making the cooling improvement even more significant.
Apple’s rumoured iPhone game controller could unlock better sustained gaming performance
This could become even more interesting going forward. A recent report claims Apple is developing two dedicated iPhone game controllers, with references pointing to features such as dual thumbsticks, a D-pad, analog triggers, haptics and potentially motion controls.
If Apple’s upcoming rumoured iPhone game controller also incorporates some form of active cooling, the iPhone could become a genuinely interesting handheld gaming platform. The A20 Pro already delivers strong sustained performance with passive cooling, so an external fan or cooling plate could potentially help it maintain higher clocks and power levels for longer.

title.en: 6 Old-School Pony Cars That Aren't The Ford Mustang

summary.en: Besides the Mustang, pony cars of the 1970s inclued the Mercury Cougar, Plymouth Barracuda / 'Cuda, Dodge Challenger, Chevy Camaro, and AMC Javelin.

content.en:
6 Old-School Pony Cars That Aren't The Ford Mustang
The Mustang is one of the most recognized nameplates in the automotive industry, and undeniably the face of the pony car breed, despite not being first to market. Launched for the 1964 model year, the first-gen model was designed as a low-cost performance car for younger buyers. It proved incredibly popular, with Ford selling a whopping 400,000 during its first year. Crucially, though, the Mustang provoked an answer from its rivals.
It didn't take long before they responded — in the next few years, every big American car brand had a pony car in its lineup. Like the Mustang, these models were affordable, but they also started an arms race of unhinged big-block displacement capacities. Soon, this high-horsepower contagion encompassed the whole segment and gave us icons like the Plymouth Hemi 'Cuda, Chevrolet Camaro ZL1, and Pontiac Firebird Trans Am.
In this piece, we'll have a closer look at these models, plus other early-era pony cars — not just the high-performance variants, but also the base models and mid-range V8 options. Please note: We'll list gross instead of net horsepower ratings, as they were relevant for the time. In today's horsepower currency, these figures would be much lower. With that sorted out, let's dig into the thrifty sixes, sweet-spot small blocks, and homologated big-block screamers that shaped the pony-car segment.
1967 to 1973 Mercury Cougar
In an alternate reality, Ford Motor Company's first pony car would've been Mercury-badged. Although it's remembered as Mustang's posh sibling, the Cougar was on the drawing board first. In the end, however, Mercury's team continued working on the project only after the Mustang was launched.
Unsurprisingly, Ford's premium arm used Mustang's platform, but added 3 inches to Cougar's wheelbase and equipped it with a softer-riding suspension and more sound deadening. As a result, the Cougar was more comfortable to sit and ride in, with the higher-quality interior creating a more upscale ambiance. The Cougar looked the part, too, with a striking full-width grille, hidden headlights, and wide slotted taillights.
The Cougar might've been comfort-oriented, but it didn't miss on Mustang's high-performance V8 engines. Initially it came with the 289-cubic-inch small block V8 that produced up to 225 horsepower with a four-barrel carburetor, and a 390-cubic-inch big-block V8s with as much as 325 hp. A year later, the Cougar GT-E secured the legendary 427-cubic-inch V8, which wasn't available in the Mustang, making 390 hp. The 428-cubic-inch Cobra Jet V8 engine was also available, though it was rated at lower 340 hp. In 1969, Mercury gave customers another option with the 351-cubic-inch Windsor V8 (290 hp), and later threw the 351-cubic-inch Cleveland, Boss 302, and 429 CJ engines into the fray.
Buyers could choose most of these power trains with the optional XR-7G package, which improved on the Cougar's looks with new wheels, hood scoop/pins, and an upmarket interior. Still, it's the Cougar GT-E that's the most performance-oriented, as it was also equipped with better suspension and brakes. Unfortunately, while manual transmissions were available, most Cougars were sold with automatics.
1964 to 1974 Plymouth Barracuda / 'Cuda
The Mustang is considered the pony car pioneer, but the Plymouth Barracuda beat it to the punch by 16 days. Still, Plymouth's competitor was based on an economy car (the Valiant), so it wasn't nearly as successful as the Mustang. Yes, it had some highlights, like a 273-cubic-inch V8 with 180 horsepower and later a 225-cubic-inch slant-6 with 235 hp, but it wasn't until the second generation arrived that the Barracuda truly took off.
Launched for the 1967 model year, the second-gen Barracuda was again based on the Valiant, but had a brand-new design and more engine options. Plymouth added a 383-cubic-inch V8 with 280 hpupgraded to 300 hp for 1968 in the Super Commando variant. Plymouth also replaced the 273-cubic-inch engine with a larger 318-cubic-inch V8 variant and added a 340-cubic-inch V8 to the mix.
The Barracuda finally parted ways with its compact-car roots for the third generation (1970 to 1974), based on Chrysler's E-body platform rather than the earlier models' A-body. This let Plymouth shoehorn in Chrysler's big-block V8s — the 440-cubic-inch Magnum V8 and 426-cubic-inch Hemi (385 and 425 hp respectively). Plymouth reserved them strictly for the high-performance 'Cuda models, also equipped with an upgraded suspension, wider treads, shaker hood scoop, "Slap-Stick" floor shift manual gearbox, and optional racing mirrors. These were some of the rarest pony cars, particularly the Hemi variants, of which only 652 were sold.
Due to the stricter emission regulations, the legendary big-block V8s were replaced with the 340-cubic-inch V8 (240 hp) in 1972 and then the 360-cubic-inch V8 (245 hp) in 1973. The Plymouth Barracuda was last sold for 1974 and never resurrected again.
1970 to 1974 Dodge Challenger
Dodge wasted no time delivering its version of the Plymouth Barracuda, the Dodge Challenger. It was based on the same E-body platform, but with a 2-inch-longer wheelbase and 1.5-inch-wider body. Penned by designer Carl Cameron, the Challenger looked modern and aggressive, though internally it was largely similar to the third-gen Barracuda.
Consequently, the Challenger shared the base 225-cubic-inch slant-6 with 145 horsepower, alongside the 318-cubic-inch V8 with 230 hp and the 340-cubic-inch V8 with 275 to 290 hp. Dodge also offered the same three-speed/four-speed manual transmissions and a three-speed automatic. Of course, it's the big-block variants that did the Challenger's keen design justice. The 383-cubic-inch variant was the standard engine option in the performance-tuned Challenger R/T model, producing 335 hp and 425 pound-feet of torque. The 440-cubic-inch Six Pack V8 and 426-cubic-inch Hemi engines were available as an upgrade, though only with the R/T trim.
To cope with the added power, the Challenger R/T was also equipped with a performance-tuned "Rallye" suspension with heavy-duty sway bars and brakes, dual exhaust, performance hood, and side stripes with the R/T moniker. These were necessary upgrades, as the first-gen Challenger had a very basic suspension layout and wasn't particularly good in the corners.
Like its competitors, the first-gen Challenger was hampered by the era's stricter emission regulations and higher insurance rates. So Dodge discontinued the 383-, 440-, and 426-cubic-inch Hemi V8s, leaving the 340-cubic-inch V8 with only 240 hp as the top choice. A year later, Dodge also axed the inline-6 option, and for 1974 replaced the 340-cubic-inch engine with the newer 360-cubic-inch V8 with 245 hp.
1967 to 1969 Chevrolet Camaro
A case can be made that Chevrolet, not Ford, pioneered the junior muscle car segment with the turbocharged rear-engine Corvair Monza in 1960. It proved surprisingly popular, so much so that it triggered the original Mustang's launch. Ford's pony car essentially deleted the Corvair Monza out of existence, forcing GM to rethink the formula and launch its own V8-powered pony car — the 1967 Camaro.
Developed on a frantic schedule, the first-gen Camaro wasn't a purpose-built sports car, piggybacking on the Nova's F-body platform. Still, it had the engine range necessary to compete with the Mustang, launching with eight different power trains. With up to 155 horsepower, the entry-level inline-6 variants weren't particularly potent, but the 327-cubic-inch (210 to 275 hp), 350-cubic-inch (295 hp), and 396-cubic-inch (325 to 375 hp) V8s more than made up for that.
The pick of the range, though, was the high-revving 302-cubic-inch V8 inside the rare Camaro Z/28. The small-block V8 was officially rated at only 290 hp, but the real figure was probably closer to 400. Built for Sports Car Club of America (SCCA) Trans-Am homologation purposes, the Camaro Z/28 also featured a performance-tuned suspension, front disc brakes, and four-speed manual transmission.
On the other end of the performance spectrum were the Central Office Production Order (COPO) variants, which unlocked factory installation of the 427-cubic-inch big-block V8 that pumped out 425 hp and 460 lb-ft. Perhaps the wildest COPO Camaro is the ZL1, produced at the request of the Fred Gibb Chevrolet dealership of La Harpe, Illinois. Equipped with a lighter aluminum-block version of the 427-cubic-inch engine borrowed from Chevy's Can-Am race cars, it had a monstrous 500 hp on tap.
1967 to 1969 Pontiac Firebird / Trans Am
While Ford enjoyed success with the Mustang and Chevrolet was busy developing the Camaro, Pontiac, under general manager John Z. DeLorean, was working on the Banshee — a radical two-seater sports car. It never materialized, but as a consolation prize, GM let Pontiac build its own version of Chevy's Camaro based on the same F-body platform: the Firebird.
DeLorean didn't want to be outdone by his in-house rival, so he went in a different direction. The Firebird was a more focused driver's car, equipped with stiffer suspension and more potent overhead-camshaft inline-6 engines. The base 230-cubic-inch unit produced 215 horsepower with the four-barrel carburetor — 75 hp more than the 230-cubic-inch Camaro. In 1968 it was replaced with a larger 250-cubic-inch unit that also made 215 hp. At the opposite end of the spectrum, Pontiac employed the big-block 400-cubic-inch V8. Available in several power outputs, the massive V8 offered 325 to 340 hp in the regular Firebirds and 335 to 345 hp with the Trans Am package.
Although the name suggests that Trans Am-equipped cars were homologation specials, their engines were actually too big to qualify for the championship. Instead, Pontiac bought the naming rights from the SCCA, creating one of the most renowned pony-car nameplates. The Trans Am package also carried cachet, as it brought cosmetic and aerodynamic improvements, like a big rear spoiler and ram air induction ducts. The Ride and Handling package was also included, featuring a heavy-duty suspension with hydraulic dampers, variable-ratio power steering, and front disc brakes.
1968 to 1974 AMC Javelin
The pony-car craze was so infectious during the 1960s that it even spread to American Motors Corporation, perhaps the most conservative automaker of the time. But there was nothing conservative about the Javelin, AMC's first pony car. Yes, it was based on the Rambler American, but unlike its rivals, it was built with lightness and agile handling in mind. Heck, AMC even launched a lighter AMX model with a 12-inch-shorter wheelbase and two seats, aimed at driving enthusiasts.
Initially, the Javelin was offered with 258-cubic-inch (225 hp) and 343-cubic-inch (235 hp) V8s, but AMC later offered a larger 390-cubic-inch (315 hp) V8 with the performance-oriented Go Package. For second-gen model, which arrived for 1971, AMC went a step further and introduced an even larger 401-cubic-inch V8 with 330 hp. This brought the Javelin closer to its rivals' high-performance variants, though the Javelin was also heavier than before. The AMX variant now had four instead of two seats, but it was still a V8-only affair. Buyers who wanted tidier handling could again opt for the Go Package, which included a Twin-Grip limited-slip differential, cowl induction, dual exhaust, front disc brakes, fiberglass-belted wide-tread tires, and mag-style wheels.
The second-gen Javelin AMX also brought AMC success at Trans-Am, capturing seven of the 10 races during the 1971 season to capture the manufacturer's championship, and then repeating as champ in 1972. Still, from 1972, like each of its rivals, AMC detuned Javelin's engines to comply with the stricter emission regulations, with the Javelin discontinued after the 1974 model year.
