title.en: iPhone Duo Vs. iPad Mini: Which Apple Device Is Right For You?

summary.en: An iPhone Duo can serve as your tablet and phone in one, but the iPad Mini's larger screen and better multitasking still have a place.

content.en:
iPhone Duo vs. iPad Mini: Which Apple device is right for you?
The iPhone Duo could replace your tablet, but there's something to be said for having a separate device.
The iPhone Duo is slated to arrive October 23, and on the surface, the new foldable has a lot of overlap with Apple's smallest iPad, the iPad Mini. The Duo's interface is very iPad-esque, with a similar screen size and better hardware. However, whether the iPhone Duo can truly replace an iPad depends significantly on what you need from such a device.
Ditching your tablet for a foldable phone comes with both pros and cons, especially around more complex or longform tasks. From what we've seen, the Duo manages to bridge the gap between the two technologies fairly competently. Notably, a new iPad Mini is rumored to arrive sometime soon, and reportedly brings tech specs more on par with the Duo. Since that day hasn't arrived yet, for the purpose of this discussion, we're going to compare the iPhone Duo with the most recent seventh-generation model of iPad Mini from 2024.
How the iPad Mini and Duo compare
One of the biggest deciding factors between the Duo and Mini is the vast price difference. The iPad Mini starts at $600 for the 128GB model and goes up to $900 for 512GB, with cellular-equipped models costing an extra $150. The Duo starts at $2,000 for the 256GB model and goes all the way up to $3,200 for 2TB of storage. You could purchase the new 256GB iPhone 18 Pro ($1,200), plus an iPad Mini, and it would still cost less than a Duo. With such a significant price difference, you should be absolutely certain you're interested in the iPhone Duo before purchasing. Consider trying it out in an Apple Store first to see how it feels.
Specs-wise, the Duo comes out on top in processing power, boasting an A20 Pro chip versus the Mini's A17 Pro, a 7-core GPU compared to the iPad's 5-core and 12GB of RAM compared to eight. The Duo's camera is also substantially better, with both a 48 megapixel main and ultra wide lens, compared to the Mini's 12MP wide camera. However, this stat isn't particularly compelling — if you decide to invest in an iPad over the Duo, you presumably have a phone with a better camera.
The iPad Mini wins in display size, with an 8.3-inch display compared to the Duo's 7.6-inch inner display. However, both of the iPhone Duo's screens are ProMotion displays that reach up to 120Hz, while the iPad Mini's screen is 60Hz.
Some might prefer the capabilities of iPadOS, too: although the iPhone Duo's software is different from a normal iPhone, it's still not the same as the iPadOS. At most, the Duo's OS can support an app on each half of the inner screen, while the iPad has much more robust multitasking. If you use the Apple Pencil a lot, the Duo's limited compatibility is also a point to consider, as the phone will only support the USB-C version of the device, not the Pencil Pro. Said support also won't be there at launch, but will arrive later in 2026.
Which device is the better fit for you?
These tech specs paint a clear picture: the current model of iPad Mini only has the upper hand in screen size, the unique capabilities of iPadOS and better Pencil support. If two-screen multitasking is enough for you, you don't use the Apple Pencil Pro and price isn't an issue, in theory you should get the iPhone Duo. That being said, it's worth considering that the true evolution of the Duo's crease won't become clear for a long time — it might be best to wait and see how it fares.
However, not everything is answered by a side-by-side spec comparison. A large part of what determines which of these two is better for you comes down to whether you like to separate your tech. For some people, having an iPad is ideal for spending time locked in on a project or book without the many distractions that often come with a phone. It also means you won't drain your phone battery during long iPad sessions. Conversely, if you want to switch quickly between a typical phone view and an expanded one, then just as quickly close it back up to make a phone call, a Duo is the way to go.

title.en: NVIDIA DGX Spark 64GB Launched and Big 128GB GB10 Price Increases

summary.en: The NVIDIA DGX Spark 64GB is launching with a $4999 price as the 128GB model jumps to $6950 pushed by memory pricing

content.en:
The NVIDIA GB10 ecosystem is getting a shock as NVIDIA makes two changes to the lineup. First, the NVIDIA DGX Spark 128GB family is increasing in price. It looks like that model is moving up to a $6950-ish tier, with various OEMs charging different amounts. Likely realizing this is pricing many out of the market, NVIDIA has a solution with a 64GB model at $4,999.
NVIDIA DGX Spark 64GB Launched and Big 128GB GB10 Price Increases
First off, NVIDIA says that the new DGX Spark 64GB is available from Acer, ASUS, Dell, Gigabyte, HP, and MSI on Friday, Oct. 23, starting at $4,999. We will be interested to see if the partner $4999 pricing is for 1TB or 4TB when that day comes. While NVIDIA is quick to point out that the 64GB version retains the NVIDIA ConnectX-7 200GbE networking that we have seen in the 128GB model, the price is coming as a shock to many, as the NVIDIA DGX Spark 128GB/ 4TB launched at $3999 about a year ago. The new price is $6950 for that model.
NVIDIA says you can easily cluster two new 64GB models for 128GB at around $8000, and it is enabling this easily in its software.
We built a big 8x NVIDIA GB10 128GB cluster earlier this year when we were buying nodes for around $3000 each.
It is crazy to think that it is now a $50K+ option. Still, when we did the Using the Dell Pro Max with GB10 to Profit within 12 Months piece, $6000 or so for a 256GB cluster was easy to drive value from, and that was before OpenClaw really set off the huge advancements with agentic AI. To be fair, those nodes got added to the 8x node cluster, and we run them in that pool, but we underestimated the payback period with those systems because it was just on the cusp of agentic AI.
The two 128GB node cluster is great, but we generally tell folks to get a single 128GB node instead of two 64GB nodes, given our experience running these in clusters following our scale up then out advice.
Final Words
Ok, let us get to what you are probably thinking at this point. $4999 for a 64GB machine feels quite high. $6950 for a 128GB machine feels lofty, too. Our team has been chatting about this, and $6950 puts it in the range of some of the AMD Gorgon Halo systems coming out in October. So the question then becomes: do you want similar memory bandwidth but AMD with 50% more memory capacity at 192GB, or NVIDIA with the better networking but the lower 128GB capacity point? Up to 192GB of total capacity, we would prefer staying on a single system instead of scaling out. You want to scale up as much as you can, then scale out.
Likewise, Apple will begin shipping the $10,000 256GB Mac Studio M5 Ultra soon, and that will be a very strong competitor if two NVIDIA GB10s cost more. Our lab’s M3 Ultra 512GB unit is an absolute workhorse.
Memory prices are still increasing, largely due to the models getting better, and so the value of the GB10 in terms of work that it can do is going up, but the hardware cost is rough for everyone. $6950 is almost three years of a $200/mo OpenAI or Claude subscription, but with the cloud subscriptions you are sending your data to a third party. With the latest OpenAI and Claude releases, the gap between frontier and open-source smaller models you can run locally is wider, so that is another valid point to make.
I was chatting with Patrick, our EiC and Chief Analyst, about this before doing the story. His response was, “Yikes, but we are paying $2000 for 64GB ECC RDIMMs, so pricing logically must increase.” Tellingly also, “We were far off in how fast we have been able to generate value from the GB10’s as we have been getting much more out of them than we projected.”
In October, you should see three NVIDIA DGX Station reviews on STH. The GB300-based systems currently sell for around $100K, but at some point, as the GB10’s increase in price, that gap between a GB10 cluster and the $100K bigger box gets closer. If you saw our GB300 station piece in Substack, we have those GB300 stations running in a cluster using 800Gbps networking, which was fascinating and gave us an appreciation for the scale-up versus scaling-out debate.

summary.en: Things are getting crazy in the Apple rumor world, as even though the iPhone 18 Pro and several other products have only just launched and the iPhone Duo is right around the corner, there's even more to come imminently.

content.en:
Things are getting crazy in the Apple rumor world, as even though the iPhone 18 Pro and several other products have only just launched and the iPhone Duo is right around the corner, there's even more to come imminently.
October 13 looks to be the date for an introduction of Apple's revamped smart home portfolio, including the home hub device we've been hearing about for ages. This week also saw word that Apple's supply chain is struggling to meet production yield goals for the iPhone Duo ahead of its launch, while iPhone 18 Pro owners are now getting a chance to put the devices through their paces, so read on below for all of the details!
Top Stories
Three New Apple Smart Home Products Coming on October 13
A couple of those leaked products above could be arriving very shortly, as Bloomberg's Mark Gurman says Apple will be introducing a trio of new smart home products on Tuesday, October 13.
Apple will reportedly debut its long-rumored smart home hub product, as well as the new HomePod mini and Apple TV models, and while he didn't specify how Apple will introduce them, signs are pointing to some sort of event.
Apple retail stores have reportedly also received confidential boxes that are marked "Do Not Open Until October 8" and which are likely to contain merchandising materials. It's unclear, however, if they are for the upcoming iPhone Duo launch or something related to the smart home product introduction.
Apple Smart Home Hub to Feature iMac G4-Style Design
Apple's long-rumored smart home hub will have an iMac G4-style design and a host of unique features, Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reports.
The smart home hub is said to feature a square 6-inch display, with variants that can be placed on a countertop or mounted on a wall. It features a single FaceTime camera on the front, with microphones and speakers in its connected base.
Leaks suggest the hub may be available in Silver, Space Gray, Starlight, and Rose Pink colors, and will be able to display user-customizable Photo Faces pulled from your photos library, memories, and shared albums, a feature that appears similar to what will be available for StandBy mode on the iPhone Duo.
iPhone Duo Reportedly Facing Production Problems Ahead of Launch
The iPhone Duo is reportedly facing production difficulties ahead of its October launch, with early output expected to be limited.
A person said to be close to Foxconn's supply chain told China's Jiemian News that final assembly yields for Apple's first foldable iPhone were only slightly above 60% as of September 17. The source said that, under Apple's current quality standards, it could take another six months to a year for the assembly line to reach a mature yield.
According to the source, Foxconn is repeatedly adjusting equipment, assembly processes, and production settings as it makes the iPhone Duo at scale. The source also said suppliers were waiting to see whether Apple would ease any quality requirements to accelerate production.
iPhone 18 Pro First Impressions: What Do You Think So Far?
It's been almost two weeks since the iPhone 18 Pro models launched, and we want to hear from MacRumors readers. What do you think of Apple's newest iPhones? If you upgraded from an older phone, was it worth it? What about upgrading from an iPhone 17 Pro? What problems are you running into? Anything you love so far?
MacRumors readers have already been sharing early opinions on the MacRumors forums, and there are interesting discussion threads to read through. For early reviews and hands-on images, make sure to check out the first impressions and photos thread.
Not everything has been perfect, however, as some users have been experiencing issues such as speaker crackling or popping while some iPhone 18 Pro Max users on AT&T in the U.S. have been having issues with cellular connectivity or eSIM provisioning.
Apple Planning to Launch Products Faster and More Often
John Ternus is marking one month as Apple CEO, and he is apparently undertaking efforts to restructure the company to accelerate product development and introduce new products more frequently, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman.
Ternus apparently wants Apple to "broaden its range of devices and create a leaner organization with a greater focus on engineering." One proposal under consideration is to rely less on Apple's traditional spring and fall product release cycles, and introduce new devices more quickly and throughout the year. Ternus has also purportedly indicated that Apple must become "more experimental" to remain competitive in the era of artificial intelligence.

Each week, we publish an email newsletter like this highlighting the top Apple stories, making it a great way to get a bite-sized recap of the week hitting all of the major topics we've covered and tying together related stories for a big-picture view.

content.en:
Saturday, October 3rd 2026
Used Ryzen 7 5800X3D Gets Buyer Locked Out of Valorant Due to Previous Owner's Cheating
Buying a used Ryzen 7 5800X3D CPU has apparently locked its new owner out of Valorant. Reddit user After-Cartoonist-196 posted on r/PCBaumeister that they bought the chip through the German classifieds site Kleinanzeigen and have owned it since September 21. The CPU apparently works fine. However, Valorant kicked them out at launch, even though the game ran normally on their previous processor. Riot support reportedly told them the CPU's ID was blacklisted in Vanguard on August 12 because the previous owner had cheated. The user also claims their motherboard and storage drive got flagged, and that support refused to lift the ban. However, Riot's head of anti-cheat, Phillip Koskinas, responded on X and disputed part of that. Here's what he posted:
Hardware bans last 4 months maximum, they apply only to the game cheats were detected in, and we don't ban "everything else" when we match one component. Support will give you the time remaining on request. If it were up to me, we'd have soul bans that followed them into hell.
By that timeline, this chip should work in Valorant again by mid-December. We still don't know how Vanguard tells one 5800X3D from another, since a CPU doesn't report a unique serial number to Windows. The firmware TPM inside the processor is the likely answer, since Vanguard's on-demand mode requires TPM 2.0 and Secure Boot. Riot hasn't confirmed the method. AMD relaunched the 5800X3D at $350 in June, so plenty of AM4 owners are eyeing used ones right now. Unfortunately, there's no apparent way to check the chip for a ban before buying it.

title.en: Rockstar Officially Discusses GTA 6's Open-World Map of Vice City

summary.en: Rockstar officially reveals one of the ways that GTA 6's open-world design works with Vice City and its story.

content.en:
Open-world games have gotten very good at giving players somewhere to go, but getting them to actually care about those places is a different challenge. A huge map can provide hundreds of locations and still feel strangely empty once the initial novelty wears off. Rockstar Games has spent years pushing against that problem, with games like Red Dead Redemption 2 making travel itself feel like part of the experience instead of simply something players endure between missions.
Grand Theft Auto 6 appears to be taking that philosophy even further, especially as Rockstar expands beyond the familiar streets of Vice City. Leonida is not simply a larger version of Grand Theft Auto 5's Los Santos, but a broader setting built around multiple regions, communities, environments, and cultures. Vice City remains the centerpiece, but places like the Leonida Keys, Grassrivers, Port Gellhorn, Ambrosia, and Mount Kalaga National Park give GTA 6 considerably more ground to cover (and considerably more reason to leave the city).
GTA 6's Story Won't Take Players "Everywhere" in its Open World
The challenge, according to Rockstar, is making sure players actually experience that world without turning the story into a guided tour. As Rockstar Senior Vice President of Narrative Rupert Humphries explained in an interview with Game Informer:
                        “Part of the job of the game's story is to bring the player around the map in a way that feels authentic and interesting. We don't have time to take you everywhere, but we want you to be able to explore and get a feel for most of the places, cultures, and vibes.”
Find the odd one out before the timer hits zero.
GTA 6's story seems designed to introduce players to Leonida naturally, while leaving enough of the world outside the main path for exploration. That's easier said than done because GTA 6's map is already huge, even by Rockstar's standards. Rockstar North co-studio head Aaron Garbut described Leonida as the company's biggest map “by some degree,” with the world measuring around twice the size of Grand Theft Auto 5's map. The scale alone is not what Rockstar seems most interested in, though. GTA 6 has been built around the idea that different parts of Leonida should feel like pieces of the same living place, with the journey between them being meaningful instead of simply connecting one mission marker to another.
Garbut emphasized just how much attention went into that approach, explaining that Rockstar was “obsessed about every part” of GTA 6's world, including its rooftops, alleys, interiors, and everything in between. The goal, he said, was for the new world to become a “cohesive whole” with enough density and handcrafted detail that buildings feel real both inside and out. Combined with Humphries' comments, this suggests GTA 6's open world is not being treated as scenery surrounding the story; the world itself is being used to tell players what kind of place Leonida is.
GTA 6 will still have a main story that moves protagonists Jason and Lucia through the events surrounding their criminal lives, but Rockstar's comments make it clear that the journey is only part of what the open world is supposed to accomplish. Some locations will naturally receive more attention than others, while plenty of Leonida and Vice City will remain for players to discover on their own.

content.en:
Konami teases that Belmont’s Curse won’t be the end for Castlevania
Konami has been a bit quiet with Castlevania until recently, but the publisher has teased more to come for the franchise in the future.
Castlevania stepped back into the spotlight with the special DLC made for Dead Cells back in 2023. Now in just a few days, we’ll be getting Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse – the series’ first new, major release in many years. The good news is that things won’t be stopping here.
Producer Tsutomu Taniguchi recently spoke with Famitsu about Belmont’s Curse, and also commented on the future of the series. He indicated that Konami won’t want to wait many years for a new Castlevania game to release since that could negatively impact what the company is trying to build up with Belmont’s Curse.
Our translation of the interview excerpt is as follows:
This game serves as the Castlevania series’ 40th anniversary title. Beyond the release of this title, what is the outlook and evolution of the series going forward?
Right now, we’re pouring all our energy into the release of the game before you, Belmont’s Curse. As for the specifics of the future, that’s not yet… I mean, the development of this game started partly from a sense of urgency of ‘the number of people actually playing Castlevania has gone down’, and the number of people who had heard of it, but never actually played had gone up.
So with the release of this game I thought, “Phew… we did it”, but if we said, “Okay, the next game will be out in ten years”, the whole thing is meaningless. Although, I still don’t know what shape that will take.”
Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is heading to Nintendo Switch on October 15, 2026. We just recently found out that the game will run better on Nintendo Switch 2 via backwards compatibility.

title.en: Not Completely Out Of The Blue: Introducing The Longines Spirit Pilot And Spirit Pilot Flyback With Blue Dials

summary.en: ✓ Not completely out of the blue ✓ Introducing the Longines Spirit Pilot and Spirit Pilot Flyback with blue dials in fan-favorite sizes ✓

content.en:
Not Completely Out Of The Blue: Introducing The Longines Spirit Pilot And Spirit Pilot Flyback With Blue Dials
A year after Longines debuted the refreshed and resized Spirit Pilot models, four new iterations are touching down. They’re not completely out of the blue. After the black versions, the Longines Spirit Pilot and Spirit Pilot Flyback with blue dials make perfect sense. So do the 39mm cases.
The initial black-dial Spirit Pilot and Spirit Pilot Flyback were met with much enthusiasm. Longines took the familiar Spirit recipe and, instead of adding more, toned it down. The Spirit Pilot was given its simplest form, while the Spirit Pilot Flyback brought back a key aviation complication — the flyback chronograph. A year later, these watches now come with blue dials, blue rubber straps, and, for the chronograph, a blue ceramic bezel. It’s a logical next step for the Longines Spirit Pilot. After all, anyone who has been into watches for a while knows that after black comes blue. And after blue comes…? Take a guess, and I will disclose my prediction in the final paragraph.
Introducing the Longines Spirit Pilot and Spirit Pilot Flyback with blue dials
A pilot’s watch with a black dial is a classic. But what is a pilot’s watch with a blue dial? A contemporary classic? I guess so, but the number of pilot-themed watches, from three-handers and GMTs to chronographs and even perpetual calendars with blue dials, is impossible to count. We’re living in an age when color variations are more important than ever. The times when a pilot needed a sober, functional black-dial watch are over. We’re now living in an age of desire. Plenty of people out there desire an aviation-themed watch, so brands need to keep their collections of pilot watches evolving to stay attractive. That means creating dial variations in all possible colorways. Blue is, more often than not, the first color variation to appear after a black-dial model.
Blue makes sense
Adding a matte blue dial to the Spirit Pilot and Spirit Pilot Flyback makes sense. Blue is, after all, widely considered the most popular color in the world. Longines knows this, which is why the two new models are also available with dial-matching, Swiss-made blue rubber straps. The chronograph also has a ceramic bezel insert in the color that reminds you of a cloudless sky and goes well with almost everything you wear. If that’s too blue for you, you can buy either Spirit Pilot model on a stainless steel bracelet with a micro-adjustable folding clasp.
To refresh your memory, the Spirit Pilot (€2,950 on the steel bracelet, €2,600 on the blue rubber strap) has a 39 × 47.2 × 11.5mm case and is outfitted with the L888.4 automatic caliber, featuring a silicon balance spring and components that provide magnetism resistance up to 10 times greater than the ISO 764 standard. The COSC-certified movement runs at a modern 25,200 vibrations per hour and offers up to 72 hours of power reserve. A screw-down crown and screw-in case back contribute to a 100m water resistance rating.
Silver-colored hands, applied Arabic numerals, and a refined minute track keep the matte blue dial very legible. The dial may have switched from purely functional black to more fashionable blue, but there’s still no unnecessary decoration to distract the pilot, so to speak.
Fly forth and immediately back again
The same functional approach, but in blue, is applied to the Spirit Pilot Flyback (€5,450 on the steel bracelet, or €5,100 on the blue rubber strap). In Longines’s history, the flyback function is a landmark. The company was working on flyback chronographs — watches that allow the user to restart the chronograph seconds hand from zero without stopping and resetting it first — as early as the 1930s. And Longines filed its patent for a flyback chronograph in 1935. So, even with a blue dial instead of a black one, the new watch has a legitimate historical connection to the technology rather than merely borrowing the name.
The latest version of the Spirit Pilot Flyback features a stainless steel case with a 39.5mm diameter, 47.4mm lug-to-lug, and 13.4mm thickness. Like the three-hand Spirit Pilot, the Flyback also offers 100m water resistance. As mentioned, a blue ceramic insert sits inside the bidirectional bezel and incorporates a countdown scale. Combined with the blue dial, it gives the watch a distinctly monochromatic appearance. The box-shaped sapphire crystal adds another vintage-inspired touch, while silver-colored hands and applied Arabic numerals with Super-LumiNova keep the cockpit-instrument theme intact.
A treat for fans of mechanical watchmaking
Powering the Flyback is the hand-wound Longines L792.4, and looking through the transparent screw-in case back is a treat for every fan of mechanical watchmaking. Yes, some movements have way better finishing, but you’ll also pay a price for that. Longines offers you a COSC-certified hand-wound flyback chronograph movement with an impressive 68-hour power reserve, a silicon balance spring, and a column wheel for less than €5.5k. And it comes in a very modest (read: “classic”) case size. In a world of often bulky and costly retro-styled aviation chronographs with less traditional and less pretty automatic calibers, the Spirit Pilot Flyback, in either blue or black, stands out.
By adding blue-dial versions to the Spirit Pilot lineup, Longines once again strengthened the Spirit collection. The two more contemporary blue models are a welcome addition to last year’s black enthusiast editions. I’m guessing that in 2027, we will see the launch of both the Longines Spirit Pilot and Spirit Pilot Flyback with green dials. What do you think? And do you like these blue versions? Please let me know in the comments section below.

summary.en: It solves my biggest living room pet peeve.

content.en:
We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
I love watching television. A very high percentage of my evenings are spent taking in movies and shows. Yet, for someone so committed to TV, I really don’t want one to be the focal point of my living room. Thankfully, IKEA has come up with a particularly clever solution, and, unexpectedly, I have XBOX to thank.
The new nine-piece YXSTABY collection, which is in stores now and available online next month, was designed by IKEA and XBOX around the idea that gaming no longer happens in a dedicated room or even necessarily in one place. But you don’t need to be a gamer to appreciate its smartest small-space idea: IKEA’s first-ever rolling TV stand.
The minimalist stand can move from room to room, while built-in storage at the back gives cords, consoles, remotes, and other unsightly necessities somewhere to live. At just $150 and compatible with TVs up to 55 inches, the sleek, powder-coated steel frame is a great deal, too. title.en: Apple changes full-disk access permissions to curb abuse from AI agents

summary.en: Meta says FDA isn't sufficient to Muse reading messages. Apple begs to differ.

content.en:
Apple says it is changing its macOS privacy settings to stop third-party app developers from misusing them to access message histories.
Friday’s announcement comes two weeks after tech columnist Jason Aten said that Meta’s new general-purpose AI agent Muse sent him an unsolicited notification referencing a thread between him and a co-worker over Apple Messages. Aten said he never granted Muse permissions to read his messages and had assumed they were off-limits. Social media last week blew up with masses of people who agreed and said the incident showed that AI assistants given access to calendars, emails, messages, shopping accounts, and other resources are akin to a skill saw or other power tool. While potentially useful, they can do real damage if not used carefully.
He said/she said
Meta CTO David Singleton joined the fray with a rebuttal that appeared solid. For Muse to access Apple Messages, a user must manually give it two privileges. One is full-disk access, a macOS system-level permission. The other is to enable a Messages connector setting in Muse.
“The Messages integration in the Muse Mac app is opt in,” Singleton said. “Your Muse can only read Messages content if macOS system-level Full Disk Access is granted and the Messages connector is enabled.”
Singleton’s implication was clear. Muse could have read Aten’s Messages communications only if he had enabled both settings, and if so, the columnist had only himself—and certainly not Meta—to blame.
Earlier this week, I spoke to macOS security expert Patrick Wardle, who questioned Singleton’s denial. His reasoning: “From a technical point of view, with FDA (full-disk access), any (non-root file), is readable, browsing history, browser cookies, chats, etc etc etc.” I asked Meta how Muse couldn’t read messages when the app had full disk access, while every other app with that privilege could. Meta PR’s only response was to requote Singleton saying: “The Messages integration in the Muse Mac App is opt-in. Your Muse can only read Messages content if macOS system-level Full Disk Access is granted and the Messages connector is enabled.”

content.en:
Nacon announced what the company is claiming is the world’s first officially licensed PlayStation 5 controller with a built-in screen for adjusting settings like joystick sensitivity or remapping buttons right on the gamepad. The Revolution 5 Unlimited’s screen can also be used to mix audio from multiple sources so while using a pair of headphones connected to the gamepad with a cable you can listen to music from your phone and sounds from the game you’re playing at the same time.
Nacon’s new PS5 controller can mix audio from your phone and console
The customizable Revolution 5 Unlimited gamepad features asymmetrical TMR thumbsticks and a built-in settings screen.
The Revolution 5 Unlimited is available for preorder starting today for $229.99 through Nacon’s online store and is expected to ship sometime later this year. While it’s primarily designed for use with the PS5, the R5U features an asymmetrical stick layout similar to Xbox and Switch gamepads with a pair of drift-resistant tunneling magnetoresistance (TMR) thumbsticks. Both sticks can be customized by attaching alternate heads featuring different designs and the controller’s D-pad is swappable. You can use a classic four-way design or switch to an eight-way option that makes it easier to perform combo moves in fighting games.
Nacon even lets you adjust how balanced the controller feels with 10, 14, and 16 gram weights that can be inserted into the R5U’s non-slip grips.
On the top of the controller you’ll find a pair of shoulder buttons, a pair of customizable shortcut buttons, and a pair of triggers with adjustable travel that can be shortened to reduce reaction times in FPS games. There’s four additional customizable shortcut buttons on the back of the controller as well as a button used for quickly switching between multiple saved profiles.
The R5U is also compatible with PCs and Android devices and customizing its performance and functionality isn’t limited to its built-in screen. Nacon also offers a mobile app for iOS and Android that expands the customization options to include adjusting the thumbsticks’ response curves, tweaking EQ profiles for the audio sources, and modifying the color of the RGB lighting surrounding the right stick.

title.en: Home Assistant renames Home Assistant Cloud to Link

summary.en: ﻿Founder Paulus Schoutsen explains why the smart home platform is dropping “cloud” from its name and how a new hub and AI agents could take it mainstream.

content.en:
The open-source smart home platform Home Assistant is kicking the cloud to the curb — in name at least. “We are renaming Home Assistant Cloud to Home Assistant Link, because we hate clouds,” founder Paulus Schoutsen told The Verge in an interview ahead of today’s announcement. “Big tech ruined the cloud, so we’re out.”
Home Assistant says ‘Big tech ruined the cloud, so we’re out’
Founder Paulus Schoutsen explains why the smart home platform is dropping “cloud” from its name and how a new hub and AI agents could take it mainstream.
The move is part of a long-term strategy Schoutsen and his team have been pursuing to make Home Assistant a mainstream smart home platform. Schoutsen says most users find the powerful platform after hitting the limits of mainstream options like Google Home, Amazon Alexa, and Apple Home. But it has a steep learning curve, and that’s what he’s looking to change.
I spoke with Schoutsen at the Z-Wave Summit in Boca Raton, Florida, this week about the changes and Home Assistant’s future plans, which include lowering barriers to entry by developing simpler dashboards, making setup more intuitive, and using generative AI to reduce complexity. He also said they plan to launch a new hub next year that’s more user-friendly. “We’re growing up.”
“You don’t have to trust me not to misuse your data because I just don’t have your data.”
— Paulus Schoutsen
Renaming Home Assistant Cloud to Link is mostly symbolic. The features stay the same, aside from some back-end improvements to speed and reliability. The new name also tries to address a concern some new users had that it meant Home Assistant ran in the cloud, says Schoutsen. Home Assistant runs on local hardware and controls your smart home locally, but this means once you leave your home network, you can’t control anything.
For $6.50 a month or $65 a year, Home Assistant Link gives you a convenient way to access your Home Assistant instance from anywhere, alongside the option to enable other internet-dependent features such as integration with Alexa and Google voice control, text-to-speech, speech-to-text, and encrypted backups.
The move addresses an awkward dynamic for the platform. Schoutsen and his team have spent years campaigning against proprietary cloud ecosystems, which he believes hurt the smart home, and encouraging people not to buy cloud-dependent products, all while offering a service with “cloud” in the name. However, unlike some cloud services, Home Assistant Cloud was never mandatory, and you could always replicate everything it provided with other methods; the same remains true for Link.
Schoutsen says Link is also different from many cloud services because it has no access to your data. Link is run by Nabu Casa, Home Assistant’s commercial partner, and all Link traffic is encrypted. “We can’t see it, and we don’t want to,“ he says. “You don’t have to trust me not to misuse your data because I just don’t have your data.” The service provides a revenue stream to fund the platform’s development, with 60 percent of the profit going to the non-profit Open Home Foundation that runs Home Assistant.
For Home Assistant, cloud-dependent products are a hard no. “The cloud is ruining how people think of the smart home,” says Schoutsen, pointing to the recent examples of Nest shutting off the cloud for its early thermostats, smart TVs sending your data to the cloud without you knowing, and Weber sunsetting the June Oven’s servers. “Now you have a dumb oven that cost $1,500. It’s crazy,” he says. “People get so used to it and get so disappointed by it.”
The cloud isn’t all bad, Schoutsen concedes. Speech-to-text, backups, and AI work better online, but the problem is products that stop working without it. He wants product manufacturers to commit to offering local control by default, using open standards (Matter, Zigbee, Z-Wave, MQTT, ESPHome), never locking basic features behind a cloud, and allowing users to control their own data.
“I’d love to see a nutrition label on boxes showing if a product is cloud-dependent or not,” he says, adding that they’re building a database to help consumers find products that aren’t fully reliant on the cloud.
This stance against the cloud is likely to appeal to consumers who are increasingly concerned about who has access to their data. But Home Assistant still has a long way to go before it becomes mainstream. Schoutsen says Home Assistant is installed in an estimated 2.7 million homes, but that’s still a fraction of the reach of Amazon Alexa, Google Home, Samsung SmartThings, and Apple Home. Winning over mainstream users will be hard.
The biggest barrier to entry is complexity. Home Assistant does a lot, meaning you have a lot of choice, which can be overwhelming. “If you want to try something with Home Assistant, the answer is never no,” says Schoutsen. “We want everything to be possible, which means that the UX is more complicated, and that scares people.” In comparison, “You open Apple Home, and there’s like nothing you can do,” he says.
Over the last few years, the team has been working to remove those barriers without taking away functionality. “We’re looking to lower the floor without lowering the ceiling,” he says. There are plans to launch a successor to the Home Assistant Green hub that will be easier to set up. “We want to make it more like onboarding a Philips Hue hub,” says Schoutsen.
They are also working to make the UX easier and will integrate the HACS community store — where users find and install community-built integrations — into Home Assistant next month. This should make integrations easier to find and set up. “If people haven’t tried Home Assistant in over a year, they should give it a shot,” he says.
“We’re looking to lower the floor without lowering the ceiling.”
— Paulus Schoutsen
Another big push that could turn into a major selling point for the platform is a “No Device Left Behind” program. Nabu Casa is developing devices that will more easily bring people’s existing analog or legacy tech into the platform — such as old receivers, AC units, solar panel inverters, even TVs — using technology such as serial, IR, and Modbus.
Schoutsen sees AI as a big driver for Home Assistant. “AI is going to solve the complexity problem, and our biggest weakness is becoming our biggest strength,” he says. As a broad, open platform that can bring together data and controls from across your smart home, Home Assistant could provide a useful foundation for AI agents.
I used Claude to set up Home Assistant last year, and it was a big improvement over trying to figure out what on earth YAML was. “Soon you’re just going to have your agent configure your software for you,” he says. “Because people don’t want the software, they just want the solution that comes out of it.” Schoutsen acknowledges that agents raise obvious privacy concerns, but says Home Assistant keeps your data at home and you can choose which agent to trust with it, including one that runs locally.
Ultimately, Home Assistant may not need to reinvent itself to win over the mainstream if it can become the foundational layer that lets your home talk to your AI agent or platform of choice. “If you just have a box in your house that runs Home Assistant that connects all your data to your agents or to, say, Apple Home, that’s great,” he says. “That’s a win for Home Assistant.”

title.en: Hands-On With QSSR: AI-Driven Upscaling for the Standard PS5

summary.en: Plus: further details from Sony's graphics R&D team. - Sony has revealed QSSR - Quick Spectral Super Resolution - bringing machine learning based upscaling t...

content.en:
Sony has revealed QSSR - Quick Spectral Super Resolution - bringing machine learning based upscaling to the standard PlayStation 5. It's a refined refactoring of PSSR upscaling available on PS5 Pro, available initially for Marvel's Wolverine and Ghost of Yōtei. We had the chance to go hands-on with the technology for around six hours a couple of weeks back and we've also spoken to Sony about how it works.
We've only seen the two games so far (video coming very soon), but the potential here is remarkable: low resolution and poor upscaling have impacted so many titles in this generation, but QSSR could make a big difference. In Marvel's Wolverine especially, the quality boost can be exceptional.
In terms of image quality analysis, suffice it to say that temporal stability is substantially improved, detail level increases, sub-pixel integrity is considerably superior, while artefacts from elements like moving foliage are much reduced. That said, with Ghost of Yotei, a game with already decent image quality saw less dramatic improvements.
The most immediate question you may have is this: why would Sony release QSSR when high quality upscaling is one of the unique selling points of the PS5 Pro? The bottom line is this: PS5 Pro has much more performance in delivering higher output upscaled resolution and higher base resolutions too. There remains a big divide between the same game running QSSR on standard PS5 and PSSR on Pro.
Daniel Craig, Principal Engineer for Graphics R&D at SIE says, "It's great to be improving the PS5 this far into the generation, enabling developers to make even better-looking games. The reality is that the PS5 Pro has 300 TOPS of dedicated hardware for this purpose and is free to pick a much more generous spot on that cost-versus-quality curve."
Refactoring PSSR for the standard PlayStation 5 is a remarkable achievement. PS5 Pro has dedicated ML silicon and PSSR, which has commonalities with AMD's FSR 4, uses INT8 instructions. The base PS5 does not support this.
"It's true that PS5 Pro was purpose built for the task, so QSSR relies primarily on FP16 math," explains Craig. "A streamlined neural network architecture got us close but from there we leveraged a variety of less obvious hardware features to maximise efficiency (as console developers tend to do)... packed math instructions are used extensively. The real challenge is keeping the pipeline full and reducing or amortising the costs around the math."
And while QSSR has many of the characteristics - and the obvious plus points - of ML upscalers, it's not a straight port. Compromises were required but Sony is happy with the final result:
"Game development is always about trade-offs, but we didn’t have to compromise as aggressively as you might think," says Daniel Craig "We keep a close eye on the cost-versus-quality curve of the model architecture, and the 'hard choice' was just deciding where to land for base hardware. We think we picked a spot that developers can afford while still providing an upgrade over standard TAA."
The key word there is "afford". None of the upscalers out there are a free lunch - they all have a computational cost and that cost needs to be as low as possible. Looking at PS5 Pro's PSSR, the upscaling frame-time is around 2ms upscaling to 4K. To ascertain the cost of QSSR, I performed three tests in total: running a Marvel's Wolverine cutscene with QSSR on and off in performance mode, uncapped with VRR. QSSR is slower than Insomniac's upscaler, to the tune of around 1.5ms to 1.8ms, upscaling a base 864p to 1440p. That amounts to an 8-10fps difference. However, in 60Hz performance mode, dynamic resolution scaling targets 60fps instead where the gap lessens significantly - internal resolution is lower to accommodate QSSR, but output frame-rate will be similar and image quality is much higher.
I then re-ran the test in fidelity uncapped mode, which targets a 2160p output - a much more challenging job for QSSR. Frame-rate is lower for this more challenging content but again, there's an 8-10fps difference. However, the frame-time "hit" of QSSR seemed to come in at 4.4ms. That's very high compared to the PS5 Pro alternative. Put simply, upscaling to 1440p is the more natural target for QSSR - which is what a lot of lower resolution PS5 games are doing anyway.
"Your intuition is spot on here," says Craig (note: we didn't share our numbers with Sony, only that 4K was somewhat more expensive.) "On PS5 Pro, developers almost uniformly output to 4K and adjust render resolution beneath it. On PS5, teams have to be more flexible, tuning not just render resolution, but also their intermediate and final presentation targets depending on the graphics mode. We provide tools and flexibility to help them find the right options for their title. It's not a one size fits all solution."
On the flip side, running Ghost of Yōtei's performance mode uncapped with VRR saw QSSR running almost identically to its stock FSR 3 implementation. It's just one game and we'd need to confirm similar input and output resolutions, but assuming QSSR is as fast as FSR 3, this makes it a highly compelling alternative for PS5 game developers. We'll need more games for analysis to see whether this is borne out.
Integration should be relatively straightforward for game makers. If their title supports PSSR for Pro, QSSR for the standard PS5 shouldn't require too much effort. "QSSR is fundamentally a drop-in replacement for titles that already support PSSR," explains Daniel Craig. "That said, tuning game settings takes a bit more time, perhaps a few days. For example, teams may need to adjust streaming settings to ensure higher quality mips are resident."
Similar to the Pro's PSSR roll-out, seeing QSSR added to existing games should also be expected. "Retrofits are relatively easy and low risk, but I am most excited about future titles which are authored with both QSSR and PSSR in mind."
It'll be down to Rockstar to decide whether QSSR and PSSR are supported in Grand Theft Auto 6 but the fact is that the tools are there to be used - and image quality was one of our few criticisms with the recent "extended look" trailer. And more generally, so many titles of this generation have pushed upscalers too hard - native 720p rarely looks attractive when scaled up to 1440p or 2160p. Now there is a potentially game-changing alternative - and we're looking forward to testing more supported titles.
